No such elaborate chronological precision is to be found elsewhere in the New Testament, and it comes fitly from him who claims it as the peculiar recommendation of his Gospel, that "he had traced down all things with precision from the very first" (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.3">Mt 1:3</reference>). Here evidently commences his proper narrative.<div eID="gen25234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25235" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1">Lu 3:1</reference>:<div eID="gen25235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cæsar--</hi>not the fifteenth from his full accession on the death of Augustus, but from the period when he was associated with him in the government of the empire, three years earlier, about the end of the year of Rome 779, or about four years before the usual reckoning.<div eID="gen25236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea--</hi>His proper title was procurator, but with more than the usual powers of that office. After holding it for about ten years, he was summoned to Rome to answer to charges brought against him; but ere he arrived, Tiberius died (A.D. 35), and soon after miserable Pilate committed suicide.<div eID="gen25237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Herod being tetrarch of Galilee--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen25238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and his brother Philip--</hi>a very different and very superior Philip to the one whose name was Herod Philip, and whose wife, Herodias, went to live with Herod Antipas (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.17">Mr 6:17</reference>).<div eID="gen25239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tetrarch of Ituræa--</hi>lying to the northeast of Palestine, and so called from Itur or Jetur, Ishmael's son (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.31">1Ch 1:31</reference>), and anciently belonging to the half-tribe of Manasseh.<div eID="gen25240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of the region of Trachonitis--</hi>lying farther to the northeast, between Iturea and Damascus; a rocky district infested by robbers, and committed by Augustus to Herod the Great to keep in order.<div eID="gen25241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene--</hi>still more to the northeast; so called, says Robinson, from Abila, eighteen miles from Damascus.<div eID="gen25242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25243" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.2">Lu 3:2</reference>:<div eID="gen25243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests--</hi>The former, though deposed, retained much of his influence, and, probably, as sagan or deputy, exercised much of the power of the high priesthood along with Caiaphas, his son-in-law (<reference osisRef="John.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.6">Ac 4:6</reference>). In David's time both Zadok and Abiathar acted as high priests (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.35">2Sa 15:35</reference>), and it seems to have been the fixed practice to have two (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Ki 25:18</reference>).<div eID="gen25244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness--</hi>Such a way of speaking is never once used when speaking of Jesus, because He was Himself The Living Word; whereas to all merely creature-messengers of God, the word they spoke was a foreign element. See on <reference osisRef="John.3.31">Joh 3:31</reference>. We are now prepared for the opening words of Matthew.<div eID="gen25245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13309"/><hi type="bold">1. In those days--</hi>of Christ's secluded life at Nazareth, where the last chapter left Him.<div eID="gen25246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came John the Baptist, preaching--</hi>about six months before his Master.<div eID="gen25247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the wilderness of Judea--</hi>the desert valley of the Jordan, thinly peopled and bare in pasture, a little north of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen25248" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7cffc24092230345316ea224ba7186c65a608eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13310"/><div sID="gen25249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13310"/><hi type="bold">2. And saying, Repent ye--</hi>Though the word strictly denotes a change of mind, it has respect here (and wherever it is used in connection with salvation) primarily to that sense of sin which leads the sinner to flee from the wrath to come, to look for relief only from above, and eagerly to fall in with the provided remedy.<div eID="gen25249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the kingdom of heaven is at hand--</hi>This sublime phrase, used in none of the other Gospels, occurs in this peculiarly Jewish Gospel nearly thirty times; and being suggested by Daniel's grand vision of the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of days, to receive His investiture in a world-wide kingdom (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>), it was fitted at once both to meet the national expectations and to turn them into the right channel. A kingdom for which repentance was the proper preparation behooved to be essentially spiritual. Deliverance from sin, the great blessing of Christ's kingdom (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>), can be valued by those only to whom sin is a burden (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.12">Mt 9:12</reference>). John's great work, accordingly, was to awaken this feeling and hold out the hope of a speedy and precious remedy. <div eID="gen25250" type="x-p"/>
entries.43cc6a16086a8e1d586e047fe0e1eb188b61e478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13311"/><div sID="gen25251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13311"/><hi type="bold">3. For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.11.3">Mt 11:3</reference>).<div eID="gen25251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The voice of one crying in the wilderness--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.3.2">Lu 3:2</reference>); the scene of his ministry corresponding to its rough nature.<div eID="gen25252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight--</hi>This prediction is quoted in all the four Gospels, showing that it was regarded as a great outstanding one, and the predicted forerunner as the connecting link between the old and the new economies. Like the great ones of the earth, the Prince of peace was to have His immediate approach proclaimed and His way prepared; and the call here--taking it generally--is a call to put out of the way whatever would obstruct His progress and hinder His complete triumph, whether those hindrances were public or personal, outward or inward. In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.5">Lu 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.6">6</reference>) the quotation is thus continued: "Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth; and all flesh shall see the salvation of God." Levelling and smoothing are here the obvious figures whose sense is conveyed in the first words of the proclamation--"Prepare ye the way of the Lord." The idea is that every obstruction shall be so removed as to reveal to the whole world the salvation of God in Him whose name is the "Saviour." (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.98.3">Psa 98:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Is 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">49:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">52:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.31">Lu 2:31</reference>, 32; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">Ac 13:47</reference>). <div eID="gen25253" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4c49daf9900886c06d4d11c3f297d95cc531760: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13312"/><div sID="gen25254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13312"/><hi type="bold">4. And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair--</hi>woven of it.<div eID="gen25254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and a leathern girdle about his loins--</hi>the prophetic dress of Elijah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.8">2Ki 1:8</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Zech.13.4">Zec 13:4</reference>).<div eID="gen25255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and his meat was locusts--</hi>the great, well-known Eastern locust, a food of the poor (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.22">Le 11:22</reference>).<div eID="gen25256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and wild honey--</hi>made by wild bees (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25">1Sa 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.26">26</reference>). This dress and diet, with the shrill cry in the wilderness, would recall the stern days of Elijah. <div eID="gen25257" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0873298b0246841dd45563479ddc496b912a5ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13313"/><div sID="gen25258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13313"/><hi type="bold">5. Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judea, and all the region round about Jordan--</hi>From the metropolitan center to the extremities of the Judean province the cry of this great preacher of repentance and herald of the approaching Messiah brought trooping penitents and eager expectants. <div eID="gen25258" type="x-p"/>
entries.442189275909c3ae7bbe8740db2089afacadecf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13314"/><div sID="gen25259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13314"/><hi type="bold">6. And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins--</hi>probably confessing aloud. This baptism was at once a public seal of their felt need of deliverance from sin, of their expectation of the coming Deliverer, and of their readiness to welcome Him when He appeared. The baptism itself startled, and was intended to startle, them. They were familiar enough with the baptism of proselytes from heathenism; but this baptism of Jews themselves was quite new and strange to them. <div eID="gen25259" type="x-p"/>
entries.93017427a8e6c542040859362874d4c035ef22cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13315"/><div sID="gen25260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13315"/><hi type="bold">7. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them--</hi>astonished at such a spectacle.<div eID="gen25260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O generation of vipers--</hi>"Viper brood," expressing the deadly influence of both sects alike upon the community. Mutually and entirely antagonistic as were their religious principles and spirit, the stern prophet charges both alike with being the poisoners of the nation's religious principles. In <reference osisRef="Matt.12.34">Mt 12:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.33">23:33</reference>, this strong language of the Baptist is anew applied by the faithful and true Witness to the Pharisees specifically--the only party that had zeal enough actively to diffuse this poison.<div eID="gen25261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who hath warned you--</hi>given you the hint, as the idea is.<div eID="gen25262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to flee from the wrath to come?--</hi>"What can have brought you hither?" John more than suspected it was not so much their own spiritual anxieties as the popularity of his movement that had drawn them thither. What an expression is this, "The wrath to come!" God's "wrath," in Scripture, is His righteous displeasure against sin, and consequently against all in whose skirts sin is found, arising out of the essential and eternal opposition of His nature to all moral evil. This is called "the coming wrath," not as being wholly future--for as a merited sentence it lies on the sinner already, and its effects, both inward and outward, are to some extent experienced even now--but because the impenitent sinner will not, until "the judgment of the great day," be concluded under it, will not have sentence publicly and irrevocably passed upon him, will not have it discharged upon him and experience its effects without mixture and without hope. In this view of it, it is a wrath wholly to come, as is implied in the noticeably different form of the expression employed by the apostle in <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:10</reference>. Not that even true penitents came to John's baptism with all these views of "the wrath to come." But what he says is that this was the real import of the step itself. In this view of it, how striking is the word he employs to express that step--fleeing from it--as of one who, beholding a tide of fiery wrath rolling rapidly towards him, sees in instant flight his only escape! <div eID="gen25263" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f93e9129ad0b4d7158f37735a4cb1bff8dda56d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13316"/><div sID="gen25264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13316"/><hi type="bold">8. Bring forth therefore fruits--</hi>the true reading clearly is "fruit";<div eID="gen25264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meet for repentance--</hi>that is, such fruit as befits a true penitent. John now being gifted with a knowledge of the human heart, like a true minister of righteousness and lover of souls here directs them how to evidence and carry out their repentance, supposing it genuine; and in the following verses warns them of their danger in case it were not. <div eID="gen25265" type="x-p"/>
entries.736486b652d143e428615acc9046d46ccb89a7db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13317"/><div sID="gen25266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13317"/><hi type="bold">9. And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father--</hi>that pillow on which the nation so fatally reposed, that rock on which at length it split.<div eID="gen25266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham--</hi>that is, "Flatter not yourselves with the fond delusion that God stands in need of you, to make good His promise of a seed to Abraham; for I tell you that, though you were all to perish, God is as able to raise up a seed to Abraham out of those stones as He was to take Abraham himself out of the rock whence he was hewn, out of the hole of the pit whence he was digged" (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Is 51:1</reference>). Though the stern speaker may have pointed as he spoke to the pebbles of the bare clay hills that lay around (so Stanley's Sinai and Palestine), it was clearly the calling of the Gentiles--at that time stone-dead in their sins, and quite as unconscious of it--into the room of unbelieving and disinherited Israel that he meant thus to indicate (see <reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Mt 21:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">Ro 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.30">30</reference>). <div eID="gen25267" type="x-p"/>
entries.196a97e9354e6576b3fb86f5e95b694c7566b177: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13318"/><div sID="gen25268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13318"/><hi type="bold">10. And now also--</hi>And even already.<div eID="gen25268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the axe is laid unto--</hi>"lieth at."<div eID="gen25269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the root of the trees--</hi>as it were ready to strike: an expressive figure of impending judgment, only to be averted in the way next described.<div eID="gen25270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire--</hi>Language so personal and individual as this can scarcely be understood of any national judgment like the approaching destruction of Jerusalem, with the breaking up of the Jewish polity and the extrusion of the chosen people from their peculiar privileges which followed it; though this would serve as the dark shadow, cast before, of a more terrible retribution to come. The "fire," which in another verse is called "unquenchable," can be no other than that future "torment" of the impenitent whose "smoke ascendeth up for ever and ever," and which by the Judge Himself is styled "everlasting punishment" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.46">Mt 25:46</reference>). What a strength, too, of just indignation is in that word "cast" or "flung into the fire!"<div eID="gen25271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25272" type="x-p"/> The third Gospel here adds the following important particulars in <reference osisRef="Luke.3.10-Luke.3.16">Lu 3:10-16</reference>.<div eID="gen25272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25273" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.10">Lu 3:10</reference>:<div eID="gen25273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the people--</hi>the multitudes.<div eID="gen25274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">asked him, saying, What shall we do then?--</hi>that is, to show the sincerity of our repentance.<div eID="gen25275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25276" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.11">Lu 3:11</reference>:<div eID="gen25276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat--</hi>provisions, victuals.<div eID="gen25277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him do likewise--</hi>This is directed against the reigning avarice and selfishness. (Compare the corresponding precepts of the Sermon on the Mount, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.40-Matt.5.42">Mt 5:40-42</reference>).<div eID="gen25278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25279" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.12">Lu 3:12</reference>:<div eID="gen25279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Then came also the publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master--</hi>Teacher.<div eID="gen25280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what shall we do?--</hi>In what special way is the genuineness of our repentance to be manifested?<div eID="gen25281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25282" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.13">Lu 3:13</reference>:<div eID="gen25282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you--</hi>This is directed against that extortion which made the publicans a byword. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.46">Mt 5:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.1">Lu 15:1</reference>).<div eID="gen25283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25284" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.14">Lu 3:14</reference>:<div eID="gen25284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the soldiers--</hi>rather, "And soldiers"--the word means "soldiers on active duty."<div eID="gen25285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">likewise demanded--</hi>asked.<div eID="gen25286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man--</hi>Intimidate. The word signifies to "shake thoroughly," and refers probably to the extorting of money or other property.<div eID="gen25287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither accuse any falsely--</hi>by acting as informers vexatiously on frivolous or false pretexts.<div eID="gen25288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and be content with your wages--</hi>or "rations." We may take this, say Webster and Wilkinson, as a warning against mutiny, which the officers attempted to suppress by largesses and donations. And thus the "fruits" which would evidence their repentance were just resistance to the reigning sins--particularly of the class to which the penitent belonged--and the manifestation of an opposite spirit.<div eID="gen25289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25290" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.15">Lu 3:15</reference>:<div eID="gen25290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And as the people were in expectation--</hi>in a state of excitement, looking for something new<div eID="gen25291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and all men mused in their hearts of John, whether he were the Christ, or not--</hi>rather, "whether he himself might be the Christ." The structure of this clause implies that they could hardly think it, but yet could not help asking themselves whether it might not be; showing both how successful he had been in awakening the expectation of Messiah's immediate appearing, and the high estimation and even reverence, which his own character commanded.<div eID="gen25292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25293" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.16">Lu 3:16</reference>:<div eID="gen25293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">John answered--</hi>either to that deputation from Jerusalem, of which we read in <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>, &c., or on some other occasion, to remove impressions derogatory to his blessed Master, which he knew to be taking hold of the popular mind.<div eID="gen25294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying unto them all--</hi>in solemn protestation.<div eID="gen25295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25296" type="x-p"/> (We now return to the first Gospel.) <div eID="gen25296" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cb1b8d2b95e9aa4577eec347eb089ee54a7df01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13319"/><div sID="gen25297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13319"/><hi type="bold">11. I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.6">Mt 3:6</reference>);<div eID="gen25297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he that cometh after me is mightier than I--</hi>In Mark and Luke this is more emphatic--"But there cometh the Mightier than I" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.7">Mr 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.16">Lu 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen25298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose shoes--</hi>sandals.<div eID="gen25299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am not worthy to bear--</hi>The sandals were tied and untied, and borne about by the meanest servants.<div eID="gen25300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall baptize you--</hi>the emphatic "He": "He it is," to the exclusion of all others, "that shall baptize you."<div eID="gen25301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the Holy Ghost--</hi>"So far from entertaining such a thought as laying claim to the honors of Messiahship, the meanest services I can render to that 'Mightier than I that is coming after me' are too high an honor for me; I am but the servant, but the Master is coming; I administer but the outward symbol of purification; His it is, as His sole prerogative, to dispense the inward reality." Beautiful spirit, distinguishing this servant of Christ throughout!<div eID="gen25302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and with fire--</hi>To take this as a distinct baptism from that of the Spirit--a baptism of the impenitent with hell-fire--is exceedingly unnatural. Yet this was the view of Origen among the Fathers; and among moderns, of Neander, Meyer, De Wette, and Lange. Nor is it much better to refer it to the fire of the great day, by which the earth and the works that are therein shall be burned up. Clearly, as we think, it is but the fiery character of the Spirit's operations upon the soul--searching, consuming, refining, sublimating--as nearly all good interpreters understand the words. And thus, in two successive clauses, the two most familiar emblems--water and fire--are employed to set forth the same purifying operations of the Holy Ghost upon the soul. <div eID="gen25303" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc8d8c91b9b51efb9a777acc235a40acc3ee6f4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13320"/><div sID="gen25304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13320"/><hi type="bold">12. Whose fan--</hi>winnowing fan.<div eID="gen25304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is in his hand--</hi>ready for use. This is no other than the preaching of the Gospel, even now beginning, the effect of which would be to separate the solid from the spiritually worthless, as wheat, by the winnowing fan, from the chaff. (Compare the similar representation in Mal 3:1-3).<div eID="gen25305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he will throughly purge his floor--</hi>threshing-floor; that is, the visible Church.<div eID="gen25306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and gather his wheat--</hi>His true-hearted saints; so called for their solid worth (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Am 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Lu 22:31</reference>).<div eID="gen25307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the garner--</hi>"the kingdom of their Father," as this "garner" or "barn" is beautifully explained by our Lord in the parable of the wheat and the tares (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">Mt 13:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">43</reference>).<div eID="gen25308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he will burn up the chaff--</hi>empty, worthless professors of religion, void of all solid religious principle and character (see <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen25309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with unquenchable fire--</hi>Singular is the strength of this apparent contradiction of figures:--to be burnt up, but with a fire that is unquenchable; the one expressing the utter destruction of all that constitutes one's true life, the other the continued consciousness of existence in that awful condition.<div eID="gen25310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> Luke adds the following important particulars (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.18-Luke.3.20">Lu 3:18-20</reference>):<div eID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.18">Lu 3:18</reference>:<div eID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And many other things in his exhortation preached he unto the people--</hi>showing that we have here but an abstract of his teaching. Besides what we read in <reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>, 33, 34; 3:27-36, the incidental allusion to his having taught his disciples to pray (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.1">Lu 11:1</reference>)--of which not a word is said elsewhere--shows how varied his teaching was.<div eID="gen25313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.19">Lu 3:19</reference>:<div eID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But Herod the tetrarch, being reproved by him for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done--</hi>In this last clause we have an important fact, here only mentioned, showing how thoroughgoing was the fidelity of the Baptist to his royal hearer, and how strong must have been the workings of conscience in that slave of passion when, notwithstanding such plainness, he "did many things, and heard John gladly" (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.20">Mr 6:20</reference>).<div eID="gen25315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.20">Lu 3:20</reference>:<div eID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Added yet this above all, that he shut up John in prison--</hi>This imprisonment of John, however, did not take place for some time after this; and it is here recorded merely because the Evangelist did not intend to recur to his history till he had occasion to relate the message which he sent to Christ from his prison at Machærus (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.18">Lu 7:18</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen25317" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.3.13-Matt.3.17">Mt 3:13-17</reference>. Baptism of Christ and Descent of the Spirit upon Him Immediately Thereafter. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.1.9-Mark.1.11">Mr 1:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.21">Lu 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.31-John.1.34">Joh 1:31-34</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25318" type="x-p"/> Baptism of Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.13-Matt.3.15">Mt 3:13-15</reference>). <div eID="gen25318" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f95e180a6c360e96df47ec4b841c764f62f66fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13321"/><div sID="gen25319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13321"/><hi type="bold">13. Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him--</hi>Moses rashly anticipated the divine call to deliver his people, and for this was fain to flee the house of bondage, and wait in obscurity for forty years more (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.11">Ex 2:11</reference>, &c.). Not so this greater than Moses. All but thirty years had He now spent in privacy at Nazareth, gradually ripening for His public work, and calmly awaiting the time appointed of the Father. Now it had arrived; and this movement from Galilee to Jordan is the step, doubtless, of deepest interest to all heaven since that first one which brought Him into the world. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.21">Lu 3:21</reference>) has this important addition--"Now when all the people were baptized, it came to pass, that Jesus being baptized," &c.--implying that Jesus waited till all other applicants for baptism that day had been disposed of, ere He stepped forward, that He might not seem to be merely one of the crowd. Thus, as He rode into Jerusalem upon an ass "whereon yet never man sat" (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.30">Lu 19:30</reference>), and lay in a sepulchre "wherein was never man yet laid" (<reference osisRef="John.19.41">Joh 19:41</reference>), so in His baptism, too. He would be "separate from sinners." <div eID="gen25319" type="x-p"/>
entries.130b655c341b5f9b54ab9762c92112eec1cfe0d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13322"/><div sID="gen25320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13322"/><hi type="bold">14. But John forbade him--</hi>rather, "was (in the act of) hindering him," or "attempting to hinder him."<div eID="gen25320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?--</hi>(How John came to recognize Him, when he says he knew Him not, see on John 1. 31-34.) The emphasis of this most remarkable speech lies all in the pronouns: "What! Shall the Master come for baptism to the servant--the sinless Saviour to a sinner?" That thus much is in the Baptist's words will be clearly seen if it be observed that he evidently regarded Jesus as Himself needing no purification but rather qualified to impart it to those who did. And do not all his other testimonies to Christ fully bear out this sense of the words? But it were a pity if, in the glory of this testimony to Christ, we should miss the beautiful spirit in which it was borne--"Lord, must I baptize Thee? Can I bring myself to do such a thing?"--reminding us of Peter's exclamation at the supper table, "Lord, dost Thou wash my feet?" while it has nothing of the false humility and presumption which dictated Peter's next speech. "Thou shalt never wash my feet" (<reference osisRef="John.13.6">Joh 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.13.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen25321" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5e1723f3f54b959a8a9dd6807d1a9fbfa260a2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13323"/><div sID="gen25322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13323"/><hi type="bold">15. And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now--</hi>"Let it pass for the present"; that is, "Thou recoilest, and no wonder, for the seeming incongruity is startling; but in the present case do as thou art bidden."<div eID="gen25322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thus it becometh us--</hi>"us," not in the sense of "me and thee," or "men in general," but as in <reference osisRef="John.3.11">Joh 3:11</reference>.<div eID="gen25323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to fulfil all righteousness--</hi>If this be rendered, with Scrivener, "every ordinance," or, with Campbell, "every institution," the meaning is obvious enough; and the same sense is brought out by "all righteousness," or compliance with everything enjoined, baptism included. Indeed, if this be the meaning, our version perhaps best brings out the force of the opening word "Thus." But we incline to think that our Lord meant more than this. The import of circumcision and of baptism seems to be radically the same. And if our remarks on the circumcision of our Lord (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.21-Luke.2.24">Lu 2:21-24</reference>) are well founded, He would seem to have said, "Thus do I impledge Myself to the whole righteousness of the Law--thus symbolically do enter on and engage to fulfil it all." Let the thoughtful reader weigh this.<div eID="gen25324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Then he suffered him--</hi>with true humility, yielding to higher authority than his own impressions of propriety.<div eID="gen25325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25326" type="x-p"/> Descent of the Spirit upon the Baptized Redeemer (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Mt 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen25326" type="x-p"/>
entries.66fbc5542360928a40084437305f99b4fa885216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13324"/><div sID="gen25327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13324"/><hi type="bold">16. And Jesus when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water--</hi>rather, "from the water." Mark has "out of the water" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.10">Mr 1:10</reference>). "and"--adds Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.21">Lu 3:21</reference>), "while He was praying"; a grand piece of information. Can there be a doubt about the burden of that prayer; a prayer sent up, probably, while yet in the water--His blessed head suffused with the baptismal element; a prayer continued likely as He stepped out of the stream, and again stood upon the dry ground; the work before Him, the needed and expected Spirit to rest upon Him for it, and the glory He would then put upon the Father that sent Him--would not these fill His breast, and find silent vent in such form as this?--"Lo, I come; I delight to do Thy will, O God. Father, glorify Thy name. Show Me a token for good. Let the Spirit of the Lord God come upon Me, and I will preach the Gospel to the poor, and heal the broken-hearted, and send forth judgment unto victory." While He was yet speaking--<div eID="gen25327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lo, the heavens were opened--</hi>Mark says, sublimely, "He saw the heavens cleaving" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.10">Mr 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen25328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he saw the Spirit of God descending--</hi>that is, He only, with the exception of His honored servant, as he tells us himself (<reference osisRef="John.1.32-John.1.34">Joh 1:32-34</reference>); the by-standers apparently seeing nothing.<div eID="gen25329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like a dove, and lighting upon him--</hi>Luke says, "in a bodily shape" (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.22">Lu 3:22</reference>); that is, the blessed Spirit, assuming the corporeal form of a dove, descended thus upon His sacred head. But why in this form? The Scripture use of this emblem will be our best guide here. "My dove, my undefiled is one," says the Song of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Song.6.9">So 6:9</reference>). This is chaste purity. Again, "Be ye harmless as doves," says Christ Himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>). This is the same thing, in the form of inoffensiveness towards men. "A conscience void of offense toward God and toward men" (<reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Ac 24:16</reference>) expresses both. Further, when we read in the Song of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">So 2:14</reference>), "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rocks, in the secret places of the stairs (see <reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Is 60:8</reference>), let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely"--it is shrinking modesty, meekness, gentleness, that is thus charmingly depicted. In a word--not to allude to the historical emblem of the dove that flew back to the ark, bearing in its mouth the olive leaf of peace (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Ge 8:11</reference>)--when we read (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.13">Psa 68:13</reference>), "Ye shall be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold," it is beauteousness that is thus held forth. And was not such that "holy, harmless, undefiled One," the "separate from sinners?" "Thou art fairer than the children of men; grace is poured into Thy lips; therefore God hath blessed Thee for ever!" But the fourth Gospel gives us one more piece of information here, on the authority of one who saw and testified of it: "John bare record, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and IT ABODE UPON Him." And lest we should think that this was an accidental thing, he adds that this last particular was expressly given him as part of the sign by which he was to recognize and identify Him as the Son of God: "And I <hi type="bold">knew Him not: but He that sent me to baptize with water, the same said unto me, Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending AND REMAINING ON Him, the same is He which baptizeth with the Holy Ghost. And I saw and bare record that this is the Son of God" (<reference osisRef="John.1.32-John.1.34">Joh 1:32-34</reference>). And when with this we compare the predicted descent of the Spirit upon Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Is 11:2</reference>), "And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him," we cannot doubt that it was this permanent and perfect resting of the Holy Ghost upon the Son of God--</hi>now and henceforward in His official capacity--that was here visibly manifested. <div eID="gen25330" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4761163fe46ed2d62729022d0c88086d9be7771: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13325"/><div sID="gen25331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13325"/><hi type="bold">17. And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is--</hi>Mark and Luke give it in the direct form, "Thou art." (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.11">Mr 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.22">Lu 3:22</reference>).<div eID="gen25331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased--</hi>The verb is put in the aorist to express absolute complacency, once and for ever felt towards Him. The English here, at least to modern ears, is scarcely strong enough. "I delight" comes the nearest, perhaps, to that ineffable complacency which is manifestly intended; and this is the rather to be preferred, as it would immediately carry the thoughts back to that august Messianic prophecy to which the voice from heaven plainly alluded (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>), "Behold My Servant, whom I uphold; Mine Elect, IN WHOM My soul delighteth." Nor are the words which follow to be overlooked, "I have put My Spirit upon Him; He shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles." (The Septuagint perverts this, as it does most of the Messianic predictions, interpolating the word "Jacob," and applying it to the Jews). Was this voice heard by the by-standers? From Matthew's form of it, one might suppose it so designed; but it would appear that it was not, and probably John only heard and saw anything peculiar about that great baptism. Accordingly, the words, "Hear ye Him," are not added, as at the Transfiguration. <chapter eID="Matt.3"/>

entries.de7419c25d10cd206677e214bdf29381f44ed940: <div eID="gen36137" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen36138" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36139" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36139" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36138" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36140" type="x-p"/> John the Baptist begins to preach, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.1">Mat 3:1</reference>. The subject of his preaching, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.2">Mat 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.3">Mat 3:3</reference>. Description of his clothing and food, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.4">Mat 3:4</reference>. The success of his ministry, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.5">Mat 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.6">Mat 3:6</reference>. His exhortation to the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.7-Mat.3.9">Mat 3:7-9</reference>. He denounces the judgments of God against the impenitent, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.10">Mat 3:10</reference>. The design of his baptism, and that of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.11">Mat 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.12">Mat 3:12</reference>. He baptizes Christ in Jordan, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.13-Mat.3.15">Mat 3:13-15</reference>; who is attested to be the Messiah by the Holy Spirit, and a voice from heaven, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.16">Mat 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.17">Mat 3:17</reference>. <div eID="gen36140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36141" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen36141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36142" type="x-p"/> John the Baptist - John, surnamed The Baptist, because he required those to be baptized who professed to be contrite because of their sins, was the son of a priest named Zacharias, and his wife Elisabeth, and was born about A. M. 3999, and about six months before our blessed Lord. Of his almost miraculous conception and birth, we have a circumstantial account in the Gospel of Luke, chap. 1: to which, and the notes there, the reader is requested to refer. For his fidelity in reproving Herod for his incest with his brother Philip's wife, he was cast into prison, no doubt at the suggestion of Herodias, the profligate woman in question. He was at last beheaded at her instigation, and his head given as a present to Salome, her daughter, who, by her elegant dancing, had highly gratified Herod, the paramour of her incestuous mother. His ministry was short; for he appears to have been put to death in the 27th or 28th year of the Christian era. <div eID="gen36142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36143" type="x-p"/> Came - preaching - Κηρυσσων, proclaiming, as a herald, a matter of great and solemn importance to men; the subject not his own, nor of himself, but from that God from whom alone he had received his commission. See on the nature and importance of the herald's office, at the end of this chapter. Κηρυσσειν, says Rosenmuller, de iis dicitur, qui in Plateis, in Campis, in Aere aperto, ut a multis audiantur, vocem tollunt, etc. "The verb κηρυσσειν is applied to those who, in the streets, fields, and open air, lift up their voice, that they may be heard by many, and proclaim what has been committed to them by regal or public authority; as the Kerukes among the Greeks, and the Precones among the Romans." <div eID="gen36143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36144" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Judea - That is, the country parts, as distinguished from the city; for in this sense the word wilderness, מדבר midbar or מדבריות midbarioth, is used among the rabbins. John's manner of life gives no countenance to the eremite or hermit's life, so strongly recommended and applauded by the Roman Church.
entries.1eb32dc5d9a5b7879fca20e1ad4731f30b0fd88a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen36144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36145" type="x-p"/> Repent - Μετανοειτε. This was the matter of the preaching. The verb μετανοεω is either compounded of μετα, after, and νοειν to understand, which signifies that, after hearing such preaching, the sinner is led to understand, that the way he has walked in was the way of misery, death, and hell. Or the word may be derived from μετα after, and ανοια, madness, which intimates that the whole life of a sinner is no other than a continued course of madness and folly: and if to live in a constant opposition to all the dictates of true wisdom; to wage war with his own best interests in time and eternity; to provoke and insult the living God; and, by habitual sin, to prepare himself only for a state of misery, be evidences of insanity, every sinner exhibits them plentifully. It was from this notion of the word, that the Latins termed repentance resipiscentia, a growing wise again, from re and sapere; or, according to Tertullian, Resipiscentia, quasi receptio mentis ad se, restoring the mind to itself: Contra Marcion, lib. ii. Repentance, then, implies that a measure of Divine wisdom is communicated to the sinner, and that he thereby becomes wise to salvation. That his mind, purposes, opinions, and inclinations, are changed; and that, in consequence, there is a total change in his conduct. It need scarcely be remarked, that, in this state, a man feels deep anguish of soul, because he has sinned against God, unfitted himself for heaven, and exposed his soul to hell. Hence, a true penitent has that sorrow, whereby he forsakes sin, not only because it has been ruinous to his own soul, but because it has been offensive to God. <div eID="gen36145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36146" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of heaven is at hand - Referring to the prophecy of Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan 7:13</reference>,<reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>, where the reign of Christ among men is expressly foretold. This phrase, and the kingdom of God, mean the same thing, viz. the dispensation of infinite mercy, and manifestation of eternal truth, by Christ Jesus, producing the true knowledge of God, accompanied with that worship which is pure and holy, worthy of that God who is its institutor and its object. But why is this called a kingdom? Because it has its laws, all the moral precepts of the Gospel: its subjects, all who believe in Christ Jesus: and its king, the Sovereign of heaven and earth. N. B. Jesus Christ never saved a soul which he did not govern; nor is this Christ precious or estimable to any man who does not feel a spirit of subjection to the Divine will. <div eID="gen36146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36147" type="x-p"/> But why is it called the kingdom of Heaven? Because God designed that his kingdom of grace here should resemble the kingdom of glory above. And hence our Lord teaches us to pray, Thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. The kingdom of heaven is not meat and drink, says St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Rom 14:17</reference>; does not consist in the gratification of sensual passions, or worldly ambition; but is righteousness, peace, and joy, in the Holy Ghost. Now what can there be more than this in glory? Righteousness, without mixture of sin; peace, without strife or contention; joy, in the Holy Ghost, spiritual joy, without mixture of misery! And all this, it is possible, by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, to enjoy here below. How then does heaven itself differ from this state? Answer. It makes the righteousness eternal, the peace eternal, and the joy eternal. This is the heaven of heavens! The phrase, kingdom of heaven, מלכות שמים malcuth shamayim, is frequently used by the rabbinical writers, and always means, the purity of the Divine worship, and the blessedness which a righteous man feels when employed in it. <div eID="gen36147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36148" type="x-p"/> It is farther added, This kingdom is at hand. The dispensation of the glorious Gospel was now about to be fully opened, and the Jews were to have the first offers of salvation. This kingdom is also at hand to us; and wherever Christ crucified is preached, there is salvation to be found. Jesus is proclaimed to thee, O man! as infinitely able and willing to save. Believe in his name - cast thy soul upon his atonement, and enter into rest!
entries.1fe70c947ffbcb7a3ff505de744ef2265a425bc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen36148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36149" type="x-p"/> The voice of one crying in the wilderness - Or, A voice of a crier in the wilderness. This is quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>, which clearly proves that John the Baptist was the person of whom the prophet spoke. <div eID="gen36149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36150" type="x-p"/> The idea is taken from the practice of eastern monarchs, who, whenever they entered upon an expedition, or took a journey through a desert country, sent harbingers before them, to prepare all things for their passage; and pioneers to open the passes, to level the ways, and to remove all impediments. The officers appointed to superintend such preparations were called by the Latins, stratores. <div eID="gen36150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36151" type="x-p"/> Diodorus's account of the march of Semiramis into Media and Persia, will give us a clear notion of the preparation of the way for a royal expedition. "In her march to Ecbatane, she came to the Zarcean mountain, which, extending many furlongs, and being full of craggy precipices and deep hollows, could not be passed without making a great compass about. Being therefore desirous of leaving an everlasting memorial of herself, as well as shortening the way, she ordered the precipices to be digged down, and the hollows to be filled up; and, at a great expense, she made a shorter and more expeditious road, which, to this day, is called from her, The road of Semiramis. Afterwards she went into Persia, and all the other countries of Asia, subject to her dominion; and, wherever she went, she ordered the mountains and precipices to be leveled, raised causeways in the plain country, and, at a great expense, made the ways passable." Diod. Sic. lib. ii. and Bp. Lowth. <div eID="gen36151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36152" type="x-p"/> The Jewish Church was that desert country, to which John was sent, to announce the coming of the Messiah. It was destitute at that time of all religious cultivation, and of the spirit and practice of piety; and John was sent to prepare the way of the Lord, by preaching the doctrine of repentance. The desert is therefore to be considered as affording a proper emblem of the rude state of the Jewish Church, which is the true wilderness meant by the prophet, and in which John was to prepare the way of the promised Messiah. The awful importance of the matter, and the vehemence of the manner of the Baptist's preaching, probably acquired him the character of the crier, Βοων. For the meaning of the word John, see the note on <reference osisRef="Mar.1.4">Mar 1:4</reference>.
entries.ea60cfca7ed2d063a58c3c375b17779d43b5b7d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen36152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36153" type="x-p"/> His raiment of camel's hair - A sort of coarse or rough covering, which, it appears, was common to the prophets, <reference osisRef="Zac.13.4">Zac 13:4</reference>. In such a garment we find Elijah clothed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.8">2Kgs 1:8</reference>. And as John had been designed under the name of this prophet, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.5">Mal 4:5</reference>, whose spirit and qualifications he was to possess, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.17">Luk 1:17</reference>, he took the same habit and lived in the same state of self-denial. <div eID="gen36153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36154" type="x-p"/> His meat was locusts - Ακριδες. Ακρις may either signify the insect called the locust, which still makes a part of the food in the land of Judea; or the top of a plant. Many eminent commentators are of the latter opinion; but the first is the most likely. The Saxon translator has grasshoppers. <div eID="gen36154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36155" type="x-p"/> Wild honey - Such as he got in the rocks and hollows of trees, and which abounded in Judea: see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.26">1Sam 14:26</reference>. It is most likely that the dried locusts, which are an article of food in Asiatic countries to the present day, were fried in the honey, or compounded in some manner with it. The Gospel according to the Hebrews, as quoted by Epiphanius, seems to have taken a similar view of the subject, as it adds here to the text, Ου η γευσις ην του μαννα, ως εγκρις εν ελαιω. And its taste was like manna, as a sweet cake baked in oil.
entries.4db54b616e3ca50f0351daa874dee7a670a6ab36: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen36155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36156" type="x-p"/> Jordan - Many of the best MSS. and versions, with <reference osisRef="Mar.1.5">Mar 1:5</reference>, add ποταμω, the river Jordan; but the definitive article, with which the word is generally accompanied, both in the Hebrew and the Greek, is, sufficient; and our article the, which should ever be used in the translation, expresses the force of the other.
entries.9aefe1286a587bc09cb2c06ac5a7708485987b86: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen36156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36157" type="x-p"/> Were baptized - In what form baptism was originally administered, has been deemed a subject worthy of serious dispute. Were the people dipped or sprinkled? for it is certain βαπτω and βαπτιζω mean both. They were all dipped, say some. Can any man suppose that it was possible for John to dip all the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judea, and of all the country round about the Jordan? Were both men and women dipped, for certainly both came to his baptism? This could never have comported either with safety or with decency. Were they dipped in their clothes? This would have endangered their lives, if they had not with them change of raiment: and as such a baptism as John's (however administered) was, in several respects, a new thing in Judea, it is not at all likely that the people would come thus provided. But suppose these were dipped, which I think it would be impossible to prove, does it follow that, in all regions of the world, men and women must be dipped, in order to be evangelically baptized? In the eastern countries, bathings were frequent, because of the heat of the climate, it being there so necessary to cleanliness and health; but could our climate, or a more northerly one, admit of this with safety, for at least three-fourths of the year? We may rest assured that it could not. And may we not presume, that if John had opened his commission in the north of Great Britain, for many months of the year, he would have dipped neither man nor woman, unless he could have procured a tepid bath? Those who are dipped or immersed in water, in the name of the Holy Trinity, I believe to be evangelically baptized - those who are washed or sprinkled with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, I believe to be equally so; and the repetition of such a baptism I believe to be profane. Others have a right to believe the contrary, if they see good. After all, it is the thing signified, and not the mode, which is the essential part of the sacrament. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mar.10.16">Mar 10:16</reference>. <div eID="gen36157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36158" type="x-p"/> Confessing their sins - Εξομολογουμενοι, earnestly acknowledging that their sins were their own. And thus taking the whole blame upon themselves, and laying nothing to the charge of God or man. This is essential to true repentance; and, till a man take the whole blame on himself, he cannot feel the absolute need he has of casting his soul on the mercy of God, that he may be saved.
entries.ec21f6d834aa31bc7b2786661fadcd92475e7071: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen36158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36159" type="x-p"/> Pharisees - A very numerous sect among the Jews, who, in their origin, were, very probably, a pure and holy people. It is likely that they got the name of Pharisees, i.e. Separatists, (from פרש pharash, to separate), from their separating themselves from the pollution of the Jewish national worship; and hence, the word in the Anglo-saxon version is, holy persons who stand apart, or by themselves: but, in process of time, like all religious sects and parties, they degenerated: they lost the spirit of their institution, they ceased to recur to first principles, and had only the form of godliness, when Jesus Christ preached in Judea; for he bore witness, that they did make the outside of the cup and platter clean - they observed the rules of their institution, but the spirit was gone. <div eID="gen36159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36160" type="x-p"/> Sadducees - A sect who denied the existence of angels and spirits, consequently all Divine influence and inspiration, and also the resurrection of the dead. The Sadducees of that time were the Materialists and Deists of the Jewish nation. When the sect of the Pharisees arose cannot be distinctly ascertained; but it is supposed to have been some time after the Babylonish captivity. The sect of the Sadducees were the followers of one Sadok, a disciple of Antigonus Sochaeus, who flourished about three centuries before Christ. There was a third sect among the Jews, called the Essenes or Essenians, of whom I shall have occasion to speak on <reference osisRef="Mat.19.12">Mat 19:12</reference>. <div eID="gen36160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36161" type="x-p"/> Come to his baptism - The Ethiopic version adds the word privately here, the translator probably having read λαθρα in his copy, which gives a very remarkable turn to the passage. The multitudes, who had no worldly interest to support, no character to maintain by living in their usual way, came publicly, and openly acknowledged that they were Sinners; and stood in need of mercy. The others, who endeavored to secure their worldly interests by making a fair show in the flesh, are supposed to have come privately, that they might not be exposed to reproach; and that they might not lose their reputation for wisdom and sanctity, which their consciences, under the preaching of the Baptist, told them they had no right to. See below. <div eID="gen36161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36162" type="x-p"/> O generation of vipers - Γεννηματα εχιδνων. A terribly expressive speech. A serpentine brood, from a serpentine stock. As their fathers were, so were they, children of the wicked one. This is God's estimate of a Sinner, whether he wade in wealth, or soar in fame. The Jews were the seed of the serpent, who should bruise the heel of the woman's seed, and whose head should be bruised by him. <div eID="gen36162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36163" type="x-p"/> Who hath warned you - Or, privately shown you. Τις υπεδιξεν - from υπο, under, and δεικνυμαι, to show. Does not this seem to allude to the reading of the Ethiopic noticed above? They came privately: and John may be supposed to address them thus: "Did any person give you a private warning? No, you received your convictions under the public ministry of the word. The multitudes of the poor and wretched, who have been convinced of sin, have publicly acknowledged their crimes, and sought mercy - God will unmask you - you have deceived the people - you have deceived yourselves - you must appear just what you are; and, if you expect mercy from God, act like the penitent multitude, and bring forth Fruit worthy of repentance. Do not begin to trifle with your convictions, by thinking, that because you are descendants of Abraham, therefore you are entitled to God's favor; God can, out of these stones (pointing probably to those scattered about in the desert, which he appears to have considered as an emblem of the Gentiles) raise up a faithful seed, who, though not natural descendants of your excellent patriarch, yet shall be his worthy children, as being partakers of his faith, and friends of his God." It should be added, that the Greek word also signifies plain or ample information. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.6.47">Luk 6:47</reference> (note). <div eID="gen36163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36164" type="x-p"/> The wrath to come? - The desolation which was about to fall on the Jewish nation for their wickedness, and threatened in the last words of their own Scriptures. See <reference osisRef="Mal.4.6">Mal 4:6</reference>. Lest I come and smite the earth את הארץ (et ha-arets, this very land) with a curse. This wrath or curse was coming: they did not prevent it by turning to God, and receiving the Messiah, and therefore the wrath of God came upon them to the uttermost. Let him that readeth understand.
entries.7f53a1c04c2ea45e9a7cd9e779ccf9680bd12d4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen36164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36165" type="x-p"/> And now also the axe is laid - Or, Even now the axe lieth. As if he had said, There is not a moment to spare - God is about to cut off every impenitent soul - you must therefore either turn to God immediately, or be utterly and finally ruined. It was customary with the prophets to represent the kingdoms, nations, and individuals, whose ruin they predicted, under the notion of forests and trees, doomed to be cut down. See <reference osisRef="Jer.46.22">Jer 46:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.23">Jer 46:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.11">Eze 31:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference>. The Baptist follows the same metaphor: the Jewish nation is the tree, and the Romans the axe, which, by the just judgment of God, was speedily to cut it down. It has been well observed, that there is an allusion here to a woodman, who, having marked a tree for excision, lays his axe at its root, and strips off his outer garment, that he may wield his blows more powerfully, and that his work may be quickly performed. For about sixty years before the coming of Christ, this axe had been lying at the root of the Jewish tree, Judea having been made a province to the Roman empire, from the time that Pompey took the city of Jerusalem, during the contentions of the two brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, which was about sixty-three years before the coming of Christ. See Joseph. Antiq. l. xiv. c. 1-5. But as the country might be still considered as in the hands of the Jews, though subject to the Romans, and God had waited on them now nearly ninety years from the above time, expecting them to bring forth fruit, and none was yet produced; he kept the Romans as an axe, lying at the root of this tree, who were ready to cut it down the moment God gave them the commission.
entries.c7b2e67854f804e102f6e6bf6696ba2e0cb98e29: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen36165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36166" type="x-p"/> But he that cometh after me - Or, I coming after me, who is now on his way, and will shortly make his appearance. Jesus Christ began his ministry when he was thirty years of age, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.23">Luk 3:23</reference>, which was the age appointed by the law, <reference osisRef="Num.4.3">Num 4:3</reference>. John the Baptist was born about six months before Christ; and, as he began his public ministry when thirty years of age, then this coming after refers to six months after the commencement of John's public preaching, at which time Christ entered upon his. <div eID="gen36166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36167" type="x-p"/> Whose shoes I am not worthy to bear - This saying is expressive of the most profound humility and reverence. To put on, take off, and carry the shoes of their masters, was, not only among the Jews, but also among the Greeks and Romans, the work of the vilest slaves. This is amply proved by Kypke, from Arrian, Plutarch, and the Babylonian Talmud. <div eID="gen36167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36168" type="x-p"/> With the Holy Ghost, and with fire - That the influences of the Spirit of God are here designed, needs but little proof. Christ's religion was to be a spiritual religion, and was to have its seat in the heart. Outward precepts, however well they might describe, could not produce inward spirituality. This was the province of the Spirit of God, and of it alone; therefore he is represented here under the similitude of fire, because he was to illuminate and invigorate the soul, penetrate every part, and assimilate the whole to the image of the God of glory. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.3.5">Joh 3:5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen36168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36169" type="x-p"/> With fire - Και πυρι. This is wanting in E. S. (two MSS. one of the ninth, the other of the tenth century) eight others, and many Evangelistaria, and in some versions and printed editions; but it is found in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.16">Luk 3:16</reference>, and in the most authentic MSS. and versions. It was probably the different interpretations given of it by the fathers that caused some transcribers to leave it out of their copies. <div eID="gen36169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36170" type="x-p"/> The baptism of fire has been differently understood among the primitive fathers. Some say, it means the tribulations, crosses, and afflictions, which believers in Christ are called to pass through. Hence the author of the Opus Imperfectum, on Matthew, says, that there are three sorts of baptism, <div eID="gen36170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36171" type="x-p"/> 1. that of water; <div eID="gen36171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36172" type="x-p"/> 2. that of the Holy Ghost; and, <div eID="gen36172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36173" type="x-p"/> 3. that of tribulations and afflictions, represented under the notion of fire. <div eID="gen36173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36174" type="x-p"/> He observes farther, that our blessed Lord went through these three baptisms: <div eID="gen36174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36175" type="x-p"/> 1. That of water, he received from the hands of John. <div eID="gen36175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36176" type="x-p"/> 2. That of the Holy Spirit he received from the Father. And, <div eID="gen36176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36177" type="x-p"/> 3. That of fire, he had in his contest with Satan in the desert. <div eID="gen36177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36178" type="x-p"/> St. Chrysostom says; it means the superabundant graces of the Spirit. Basil and Theophilus explain it of the fire of hell. Cyril, Jerome, and others, understand by it the descent of the Holy Spirit, on the day of pentecost. <div eID="gen36178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36179" type="x-p"/> Hilary says, it means a fire that the righteous must pass through in the day of judgment, to purify them from such defilements as necessarily cleaved to them here, and with which they could not be admitted into glory. <div eID="gen36179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36180" type="x-p"/> Ambrose says, this baptism shall be administered at the gate of paradise, by John Baptist; and he thinks that this is what is meant by the flaming sword, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen 3:24</reference>. <div eID="gen36180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36181" type="x-p"/> Origen and Lactantius conceive it to be a river of fire, at the gate of heaven, something similar to the Phlegethon of the heathens; but they observe, that when the righteous come to pass over, the liquid flames shall divide, and give them a free passage: that Christ shall stand on the brink of it, and receive through the flames all those, and none but those, who have received in this world the baptism of water in his name: and that this baptism is for those who, having received the faith of Christ, have not, in every respect, lived conformably to it; for, though they laid the good foundation, yet they built hay, straw, and stubble upon it, and this work of theirs must be tried, and destroyed by this fire. This, they think, is St. Paul's meaning, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13-1Cor.3.15">1Cor 3:13-15</reference>. If any man build on this foundation (viz. Jesus Christ) gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; every man's work shall be made manifest: and the fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is. - If any man's work be burnt, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as By Fire. From this fire, understood in this way, the fathers of the following ages, and the schoolmen, formed the famous and lucrative doctrine of Purgatory. Some in the primitive Church thought that fire should be, in some way or other, joined to the water in baptism; and it is supposed that they administered it by causing the person to pass between two fires, or to leap through the flame; or by having a torch, or lighted candle, present. Thus have those called Doctors of the Church trifled. The exposition which I have given, I believe to be the only genuine one.
entries.f53d844248cbd591f9f9a0ed4c5146c9fdd24e89: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen36181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36182" type="x-p"/> Whose fan is in his hand - The Romans are here termed God's fan, as, in <reference osisRef="Mat.3.10">Mat 3:10</reference>, they were called his axe, and, in <reference osisRef="Mat.22.7">Mat 22:7</reference>, they are termed his troops or armies. <div eID="gen36182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36183" type="x-p"/> The winnowing fan of the Hindoos is square, made of split bamboo; and the corn is winnowed by waving the fan backwards with both hands - "Whose fan is in his hand." <div eID="gen36183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36184" type="x-p"/> His floor - Does not this mean the land of Judea, which had been long, as it were, the threshing-floor of the Lord? God says, he will now, by the winnowing fan (viz. the Romans) thoroughly cleanse this floor - the wheat, those who believe in the Lord Jesus, he will gather into his garner, either take to heaven from the evil to come, or put in a place of safety, as he did the Christians, by sending them to Pella, in Coelosyria, previously to the destruction of Jerusalem. But he will burn up the chaff - the disobedient and rebellions Jews, who would not come unto Christ, that they might have life. <div eID="gen36184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36185" type="x-p"/> Unquenchable fire - That cannot be extinguished by man.
entries.0d7bd83cc7b02dd6f010f2fa7c49fce875a79eb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen36185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36186" type="x-p"/> John forbad him - Earnestly and pressingly opposed him: this is the proper import of the words διεκωλευεν αυτον. I have observed that δια, in composition, most frequently, if not always, strengthens the signification in classic authors. - Wakefield.
entries.cf4f69a0cab3000a6ec9faee1dad34198e382857: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen36186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36187" type="x-p"/> To fulfill all righteousness - That is, Every righteous ordinance: so I think the words πασαν δικαιοσυνην should be translated; and so our common version renders a similar word, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.6">Luk 1:6</reference>. The following passage, quoted from Justin Martyr, will doubtless appear a strong vindication of this translation. "Christ was circumcised, and observed all the other ordinances of the law of Moses, not with a view to his own justification; but to fulfill the dispensation committed to him by the Lord, the God and Creator of all things." - Wakefield. <div eID="gen36187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36188" type="x-p"/> How remarkable are the following words of Creeshna (an Incarnation of the Supreme God, according to the Hindoo theology) related in the Bhagvat Geeta, p. 47. Addressing his disciple Arjoon, he says, "I myself, Arjoon, have not, in the three regions of the universe, any thing which is necessary for me to perform; nor any thing to obtain, which is not obtained; and yet I live in the exercise of the moral duties. If I were not vigilantly to attend to those duties, all men would presently follow my example. If I were not to perform the moral actions, this world would fail in their duties: I should be the cause of spurious births, and should drive the people from the right way. As the ignorant perform the duties of life from a hope of reward, so the wise man, out of respect to the opinions and prejudices of mankind, should perform the same without motives of interest. The wise man, by industriously performing all the duties of life, should induce the vulgar to attend to them." <div eID="gen36188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36189" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint use this word often for the Hebrew משפת mishpat, judgment, appointment. And in <reference osisRef="Eze.18.19">Eze 18:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.18.21">Eze 18:21</reference>, the person who δικαιοσυνην και ελεος πεποιηκε - hath done righteousness and mercy, is he who sacredly attended to the performance of all the religious ordinances mentioned in that chapter, and performed them in the genuine spirit of mercy. Δικαιωματα is used 1 Maccabees 1:13, 49; 2:21, and in <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">Heb 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">Heb 10:10</reference>, to denote religious ceremonies. Michaelis supposes that כל חק kol chok, all religious statutes or ordinances, were the words used in the Hebrew original of this Gospel. <div eID="gen36189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36190" type="x-p"/> But was this an ordinance? Undoubtedly: it was the initiatory ordinance of the Baptist's dispensation. Now, as Christ had submitted to circumcision, which was the initiatory ordinance of the Mosaic dispensation, it was necessary that he should submit to this, which was instituted by no less an authority, and was the introduction to his own dispensation of eternal mercy and truth. But it was necessary on another account: Our Lord represented the high priest, and was to be the high priest over the house of God: - now, as the high priest was initiated into his office by washing and anointing, so must Christ: and hence he was baptized, washed, and anointed by the Holy Ghost. Thus he fulfilled the righteous ordinance of his initiation into the office of high priest, and thus was prepared to make an atonement for the sins of mankind. <div eID="gen36190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36191" type="x-p"/> Then he suffered him - In the Opus Imperfectum, quoted by Griesbach, there is the following addition, which, at least, may serve to show the opinion of its author: Et Johannes quidem baptizauit ilium in aqua, ille autem Johannem cum Spiritu. "Then John baptized him with water, and he baptized John with the Spirit."
entries.c864ea39fbad518225dc2a9c875e2b1dfe3f992d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen36191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36192" type="x-p"/> The heavens were opened unto him - That is, to John the Baptist - and he, John, saw the Spirit of God - lighting upon him, i.e. Jesus. There has been some controversy about the manner and form in which the Spirit of God rendered itself visible on this occasion. St. Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.22">Luk 3:22</reference>, says it was in a bodily shape like to a dove: and this likeness to a dove some refer to a hovering motion, like to that of a dove, and not to the form of the dove itself: but the terms of the text are too precise to admit of this far-fetched interpretation. <div eID="gen36192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36193" type="x-p"/> This passage affords no mean proof of the doctrine of the Trinity. That three distinct persons are here, represented, there can be no dispute. <div eID="gen36193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36194" type="x-p"/> 1. The person of Jesus Christ, baptized by John in Jordan. <div eID="gen36194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36195" type="x-p"/> 2. The person of the Holy Ghost in a bodily shape, (σωματικω ειδει, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.22">Luk 3:22</reference>) like a dove. <div eID="gen36195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36196" type="x-p"/> 3. The person of the Father; a voice came out of heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, etc. <div eID="gen36196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36197" type="x-p"/> The voice is here represented as proceeding from a different place to that in which the persons of the Son and Holy Spirit were manifested; and merely, I think, more forcibly to mark this Divine personality.
entries.62c876e38a4a4d37f12d5f99bd1565e6729af68b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen36197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36198" type="x-p"/> In whom I am well pleased - Εν ω ενδακησα in whom I have delighted - though it is supposed that the past tense is here used for the present: but see the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.17.5">Mat 17:5</reference>. By this voice, and overshadowing of the Spirit, the mission of the Lord Jesus was publicly and solemnly accredited; God intimating that he had before delighted in him: the law, in all its ordinances, having pointed him out, for they could not be pleasing to God, but as they were fulfilled in, and showed forth, the Son of man, till, he came. <div eID="gen36198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36199" type="x-p"/> As the office of a herald is frequently alluded to in this chapter, and also in various other parts of the New Testament, I think it best to give a full account of it here, especially as the office of the ministers of the Gospel is represented by it. Such persons can best apply the different correspondences between their own and the herald's office. <div eID="gen36199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36200" type="x-p"/> At the Olympic and Isthmian games, heralds were persons of the utmost consequence and importance. Their office was: - <div eID="gen36200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36201" type="x-p"/> 1. To proclaim from a scaffold, or elevated place, the combat that was to be entered on. <div eID="gen36201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36202" type="x-p"/> 2. To summon the Agonistae, or contenders, to make their appearance, and to announce their names. <div eID="gen36202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36203" type="x-p"/> 3. To specify the prize for which they were to contend. <div eID="gen36203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36204" type="x-p"/> 4. To admonish and animate, with appropriate discourses, the athletae, or combatants. <div eID="gen36204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36205" type="x-p"/> 5. To set before them, and explain, the laws of the agones, or contenders; that they might see that even the conqueror could not receive the crown or prize, unless he had strove lawfully. <div eID="gen36205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36206" type="x-p"/> 6.
