entries.0a04ead639c17dba8aec695d305e4fb8e38e2ef1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.7" sID="gen96665" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.7">Matthew 3:7</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And when he saw many of the Pharisees.</hi> It is here related by Matthew and Luke, that John did not merely preach repentance in a general manner, but that he also applied his discourse to individuals. And the manner of teaching will, in point of fact, be very unprofitable, if instructors do not judiciously inquire what the season demands, and what belongs to individuals. Nothing can be more unequal, in this respect, than a constant equality. <note n="261"> <div sID="gen96667" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et n' y a rien plus inegal en cest endroit, que de vouloir garder tousjours une mesme egalite</foreign>.” — “And nothing is more unequal, in this respect, than to wish to maintain always one uniform equality.<div eID="gen96667" type="x-p"/> </note> For this reason John, we are told, addressed the Pharisees and Sadducees with greater severity: because he saw that their hypocrisy, and swelling pride, rendered them liable to be more severely censured than the common people. To comprehend more fully his design, we must understand, that none are more stupid than hypocrites, who deceive themselves and others by the outward mask of holiness. While God thunders, on all sides, against the whole world, they construct a refuge for themselves in their own deceitful fancy; for they are convinced that they have nothing to do with the judgment of God. Does any one suppose, that John acted improperly, in treating them with so much harshness at the first interview? I reply: They were not unknown to him, <note n="262"> <div sID="gen96668" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Je res ond uil co oissoit bien quelles gens c’estoyent</foreign>.” — “I reply, that he knew well what sort of people they were.”<div eID="gen96668" type="x-p"/> </note> and the knowledge he had of them was derived, not from acquaintance or experience, but, on the contrary, from a secret revelation of the Spirit. It was therefore necessary that he should not spare them, lest they might return home more inflated with pride. Is it again objected, that they ought not to have been terrified by such severity of reproof, because they made a profession, in baptism, that they would afterwards be different persons from what they had formerly been? The reply is still easy. Those whose habits of uttering falsehood to God, and of deceiving themselves, lead them to hold out hypocrisy and pretension, instead of the reality, ought to be urged, with greater sharpness than other men, to true repentance. There is an astonishing pertinacity, as I have said, in hypocrites; and, until they have been flayed by violence, they obstinately keep their skin.<div eID="gen96666" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96665" osisID="Matt.3.7" type="section"/>
entries.9c0068f987c09f0d8450d8ffd27b648d24522c43: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.8" sID="gen96678" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.8">Matthew 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.8">Luke 3:8</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yield therefore fruits worthy of repentance.</hi> He confirms what I have already said, that the repentance, which is attested by words, is of no value, unless it be proved by the conduct: for it is too important a matter to be estimated lightly, or at random. And so John affirms, that the solemn declaration, which they made, is not enough, but that, in process of time, their works will make it evident, whether or not they have seriously repented. <note n="266"> <div sID="gen96680" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Si leur repentance est vraye, et si c'est it bon escient qu'ils vienent k luy</foreign>.” — “If their repentance is true, and if it is in good earnest that they come to him.”<div eID="gen96680" type="x-p"/> </note> It ought to be observed, that <hi type="italic">good works </hi>(<reference osisRef="">Titus 3:8</reference>) are here called fruits <hi type="italic">of repentance: </hi>for <hi type="italic">repentance </hi>is an inward matter, which has its seat in the heart and soul, but afterwards yields its fruits in a change of life. <note n="267"> <div sID="gen96681" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par le changement et amendement de vie</foreign>;” — “by the change and amendment of life.”<div eID="gen96681" type="x-p"/> </note> But as the whole of this part of doctrine has been grievously corrupted by Popery, we must attend to this distinction, that <hi type="italic">repentance </hi>is an inward renewal of the man, which manifests itself in the outward life, as a tree produces its fruit.<div eID="gen96679" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96678" osisID="Matt.3.8" type="section"/>
entries.724f89171cd0ee79e38b649e0a5f84e650a28147: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.9" sID="gen96682" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.9">Matthew 3:9</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And think not to say within yourselves.</hi> <hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.8">Luke 3:8</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And begin not to say within yourselves.</hi> As the import of both phrases is undoubtedly the same, it is easy to ascertain what John meant. Till hypocrites are hard pressed, they either sleep in their sins, or indulge in licentious mirth. <note n="268"> <div sID="gen96684" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils s'endorment toujours en leurs vices, ou s'egayent comme chevaux eschappez</foreign>.” — “They sleep always in their sins, or indulge in merriment, like horses let loose.”<div eID="gen96684" type="x-p"/> </note> But when they are summoned to the tribunal of God, they eagerly seek for some subterfuge or concealment, or some covering to interpose between God and them. John’s address to the Pharisees and Sadducees amounts to this: <hi type="italic">“</hi>Now that I have sharply upbraided you, do not, as persons of your stamp are wont to do endeavor to find a remedy in an empty and deceitful title.”<div eID="gen96683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96685" type="x-p"/>He thus tears from them the wicked confidence, by which they had been bewitched. The covenant, which God had made with Abraham, was employed by them as a shield to defend a bad conscience: not that they rested their salvation on the person of one man, but that God had adopted all the posterity of Abraham. Meanwhile, they did not consider, that none are entitled to be regarded as belonging to “the seed of Abraham,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.8.33">John 8:33</reference>,) but those who follow his faith, and that without faith the covenant of God has no influence whatever in procuring salvation. And even the little word, <hi type="italic">in yourselves, </hi>is not without meaning: for though they did not boast in words, that they were Abraham’s children, yet they were inwardly delighted with this title, as hypocrites are not ashamed to practice grosser impositions on God than on men.<div eID="gen96685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96686" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">God is able.</hi> The Jews flattered themselves with nearly the same pretenses, as are now brought forward insolently by the Papists. “There must be some Church in the world; because it is the will of God that he be acknowledged, and his name invoked, in the world. But the Church can be nowhere else than among us, to whom God has entrusted his covenant.” <note n="269"> <div sID="gen96687" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">D'autant que le Seigneur nous a ordonnez gardiens de son alliance</foreign>.” — “Because the Lord has appointed us guardians of his covenant.”<div eID="gen96687" type="x-p"/> </note> This arrogance was chiefly displayed by the high priests, and by others who had any share of government or authority. The common people were treated by them as profane and <hi type="italic">“</hi>accursed,<hi type="italic">” </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:John.7.49">John 7:49</reference>,) and they looked upon themselves as the holy first-fruits; just as, in our own day, mitred Bishops, Abbots, Canons, Monks, Sorbonnists, and every description of Priests, glorying in the proud title of Clergy, regard the Laity with contempt. This error, of relying too much on the promise of God, John exposes and refutes, by saying that, though God passes by them, he will not want a Church.<div eID="gen96686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96688" type="x-p"/>The meaning of the words, therefore, is: “God has made an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his seed. In one point you are mistaken. While you are worse than bastards, <note n="270"> <div sID="gen96689" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Quum sitis plus quam degeneres</foreign>.” — “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Combien qu' a la verite vous soyez pires que bastards</foreign>.”<div eID="gen96689" type="x-p"/> </note> you imagine that you are the only children of Abraham. But God will raise up elsewhere a new seed of Abraham, which does not now appear.” He says in the dative case, <hi type="italic">children To ABRAHAM</hi>, (<foreign xml:lang="el">τῶ ᾿Αβραὰμ</foreign>,) to inform us, that the promise of God will not fail, and that Abraham, who relied on it, was not deceived, though his seed be not found in you. Thus from the beginning of the world the Lord has been faithful to his servants, and has never failed to fulfill the promise which he made to them, that he would extend mercy to their children, though he rejected hypocrites. Some imagine, that John spoke of the calling of the Gentiles. This appears to me to be without foundation: but as proud men did not believe it to be possible that the Church should be removed to another place, he reminds them, that God has in his power ways of preserving his Church, which they did not think of, any more than they believed that he could create <hi type="italic">children </hi>out of <hi type="italic">stones.</hi><div eID="gen96688" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96682" osisID="Matt.3.9" type="section"/>
entries.f073ae107a5b5f72b750b98827d178479fc8dacd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.10" sID="gen96690" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.10">Matthew 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.9">Luke 3:9</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And now also the axe.</hi> After having stripped hypocrites of the covering of a vain confidence, John announces the approaching judgment of God. He had formerly said that, though they were rejected, God would not want a people: and he now adds, that God is just about to drive out unworthy persons from the Church, as barren <hi type="italic">trees </hi>are wont to be <hi type="italic">cut down. </hi>His statement amounts to this, that God has already displayed his power for purifying the Church. The grace of God is never manifested for the salvation of the godly, till his judgment first appears for the destruction of the world: and for two reasons; because God then separates his own people from the reprobate, and because his wrath is kindled anew by the ingratitude of the world. So that we have no reason to wonder, if the preaching of the gospel and the coming of Christ laid <hi type="italic">the axe </hi>for <hi type="italic">cutting down </hi>barren trees, or if the same causes <note n="271"> <div sID="gen96692" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ces deux choses mesme</foreign>;” — “these very two things.”<div eID="gen96692" type="x-p"/> </note> daily advance the wrath of God against the wicked.<div eID="gen96691" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96690" osisID="Matt.3.10" type="section"/>
entries.b6629faac9404af492cfdb174979d0c61676668e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.11" sID="gen96722" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96723" type="x-p"/>The three Evangelists relate the Baptist’s discourse in the same words. In one respect, Luke’s account is more full: for he opens it by explaining the occasion on which this discourse was delivered. It arose from the people being in danger of being led, by a false opinion, to convey to him the honor which was due to Christ. To remove, as soon as possible, every occasion of such a mistake, he expressly declares, that he is not the Christ, and draws such a distinction between Christ and himself as to maintain Christ’s prerogative. He would have done this of his own accord, by <hi type="italic">handing them over, to</hi> use a common expression, as disciples to Christ: but he takes up the matter at an earlier stage, lest, by remaining silent any longer, he should confirm the people in an error.<div eID="gen96723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96724" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He who cometh after me is stronger than I</hi> Christ is thus declared to be so far superior in power and rank, that, with respect to him, John must occupy a private station. <note n="282"> <div sID="gen96725" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">In ordinem cogendus sit</foreign>.” — “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il faut qu'il baissc la teste</foreign>.” — “He must bow the head.”<div eID="gen96725" type="x-p"/> </note> He uses ordinary forms of speech to magnify the glory of Christ, in comparison of whom he declares that he himself is nothing. The chief part of his statement is, that he represents Christ as the author of spiritual baptism, and himself as only the minister of outward baptism. He appears to anticipate an objection, which might be brought forward. What was the design of the Baptism which he had taken upon himself? For it was no light matter to introduce any innovation whatever into the Church of God, and particularly to bring forward a new way of introducing persons into the Church, which was more perfect than the law of God. He replies, that he did not proceed to do this without authority; but that his office, as minister of an outward symbol, takes nothing away from the power and glory of Christ.<div eID="gen96724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96726" type="x-p"/>Hence we infer, that his intention was not at all to distinguish between his own baptism, and that which Christ taught his disciples, and which he intended should remain in perpetual obligation in his Church. He does not contrast one visible sign with another visible sign, but compares the characters of master and servant with each other, and shows what is due to the master, and what is due to the servant. It ought not to have any weight with us, that an opinion has long and extensively prevailed, that John’s baptism differs from ours. We must learn to form our judgment from the matter as it stands, and not from the mistaken opinions of men. And certainly the comparison, which they imagine to have been made, would involve great absurdities. It would follow from it, that the Holy Spirit is given, in the present day<hi type="italic">, </hi>by ministers. Again, it would follow that John’s baptism was a dead sign, and had no efficacy whatever. Thirdly, it would follow, that we have not the same baptism with Christ: for it is sufficiently evident, that the fellowship, which he condescends to maintain with us, was ratified by this pledge, <note n="283"> <div sID="gen96727" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A este confirme et ratifie par ce signe</foreign>;” — “was confirmed and ratified by this sign.”<div eID="gen96727" type="x-p"/> </note> when he consecrated baptism in his own body.<div eID="gen96726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96728" type="x-p"/>We must therefore hold by what I have already said, that John merely distinguishes, in this passage, between himself and the other ministers of baptism, on the one hand, and the power of Christ, on the other, and maintains the superiority of the master over the servants. And hence we deduce the general doctrine, as to what is done in baptism by men, and what is accomplished in it by the Son of God. To men has been committed nothing more than the administration of an outward and visible sign: the reality dwells with Christ alone. <note n="284"> <div sID="gen96729" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La verite du Baptesme vient et procede du Christ seul</foreign>.” — “The truth of Baptism comes and proceeds from Christ alone.”<div eID="gen96729" type="x-p"/> </note> <div eID="gen96728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96730" type="x-p"/>Scripture does sometimes, though not in a literal sense, <note n="285"> <div sID="gen96731" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Improprie</foreign>.”<div eID="gen96731" type="x-p"/> </note> ascribe to men what John here declares not to belong to men, but claims exclusively for Christ. In such cases, however, the design is not to inquire, what man has separately and by himself, but merely to show, what is the effect and advantage of signs, and in what manner God makes use of them, as instruments, by his Spirit. Here also is laid down a distinction between Christ and his ministers, that the world may not fall into the mistake, of giving to them what is justly due to him alone: for there is nothing to which they are more prone, than to adorn creatures with what has been taken from God by robbery. A careful attention to this observation will rid us of many difficulties. We know what disputes have arisen, in our own age, about the advantage and efficacy of signs, all of which may be disposed of in a single word. The ordinance of our Lord, viewed as a whole, includes himself as its Author, and the power of the Spirit, together with the figure and the minister: but where a comparison is made between our Lord and the minister, the former must have all the honor, and the latter must be reduced to nothing.<div eID="gen96730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.11">Matthew 3:11</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">He</hi> <hi type="italic">shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire</hi> It is asked, why did not John equally say, that it is Christ alone who washes souls with his blood? The reason is, that this very washing is performed by the power of the Spirit, and John reckoned it enough to express the whole effect of baptism by the single word <hi type="italic">Spirit</hi> The meaning is clear, that Christ alone bestows all the grace which is figuratively represented by outward baptism, because it is he who “sprinkles the conscience” with his blood. It is he also who mortifies the old man, and bestows the Spirit of regeneration. The word <hi type="italic">fire</hi> is added as an epithet, and is applied to the Spirit, because he takes away our pollutions, <hi type="italic">as fire</hi> purifies gold. In the same manner, he is metaphorically called <hi type="italic">water</hi> in another passage, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.5">John 3:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen96732" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96722" osisID="Matt.3.11" type="section"/>

12. Whose winnowing-fan is in his hand In the former verse, John preached concerning the grace of Christ, that the Jews might yield themselves to him to be renewed: now he discourses of judgment, that he may strike despisers with terror. As there are always many hypocrites who proudly reject the grace of Christ offered to them, it is also necessary to denounce the judgment that awaits them. For this reason John here describes Christ as a severe judge against unbelievers. And this is an order which must be observed by us in teaching, that hypocrites may know, that their rejection of Christ will not go unpunished. They will thus be roused from their lethargy, and begin to dread him as an avenger, whom they despised as the author of salvation.
I have no doubt, that John intended also to show, what Christ accomplishes by means of his Gospel. The preaching of the Gospel, then, is the winnowing-fan Before the Lord sifts us, the whole world is involved in confusion, every one flatters himself, and the good are mixed with the bad in short, it is only necessary that the chaff be blown. But when Christ comes forward with his Gospels, — when he reproves the consciences and summons them to the tribunal of God, the chaff is sifted out,
“Les pailles s'en vont avec le vent;” — “the chaff goes away with the wind.”
which formerly occupied a great part of the thrashing-floor It is true that, in the case of individuals, the Gospel effects a separation from the chaff: but in this passage, John compares the reprobate to chaff, and believers to wheat The thrashing floor accordingly denotes — not the world, (as some people imagine,) but the Church: for we must attend to the class of persons whom John addresses. The mere title filled the Jews with pride,
“Les Juifs s'arrestoyent a ce beau titre de Peuple de Dieu, et d'En-fans d'Abraham, et s'en enfioyent.” — “The Jews dwelt upon this fine title of People of God, and Children of Abraham, and were proud of it.”
but John tells them that it is foolish in them to be proud of it, because they hold but a temporary place in the Church of God, from which they are soon to be thrown out, like chaff from the thrashing-floor. In this way, he gives a rapid glance at the corrupt state in which the Church then was: for it was covered with husks, and straws, and other rubbish, but would soon be cleansed by the strong breeze of the Gospel. But how is Christ said to separate the chaff from the wheat, when he can find nothing in men but mere chaff? The answer is easy. The elect are formed into wheat,
“Les esleus, qui de leur nature ne sont que paille, deviennent froment par la grace de Dieu.” — “The elect, who by their nature are only chaff; become wheat by the grace of God.”
and are then separated from the chaff, and collected into the granary
He will thoroughly cleanse his thrashing-floor This work was begun by Christ, and is daily going forward: but the full accomplishment of it will not be seen till the last day. This is the reason why John draws our attention to the subject. But let us remember, that believers even now enter, by hope, into the granary of God, in which they will actually have their everlasting abode; while the reprobate experience, in their convictions of guilt, the heat of that fire, the actual burning of which they will feel at the last day.
Many persons, I am aware, have entered into ingenious debates about the eternal fire, by which the wicked will be tormented after the judgment. But we may conclude from many passages of Scripture, that it is a metaphorical expression. For, if we must believe that it is real, or what they call material fire, we must also believe that the brimstone and the fan are material, both of them being mentioned by Isaiah.
“For Tophet is ordained of old; the pile thereof is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it,” (Isaiah 30:33.)
We must explain the fire in the same manner as the worm, (Mark 9:44, 46, 48.) and if it is universally agreed that the worm is a metaphorical term, we must form the same opinion as to the fire. Let us lay aside the speculations, by which foolish men weary themselves to no purpose, and satisfy ourselves with believing, that these forms of speech denote, in a manner suited to our feeble capacity, a dreadful torment, which no man can now comprehend, and no language can express.

entries.25094cd4f1e0b1d6dbf2a689a065b57ca4433a61: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.13" sID="gen96755" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.13">Matthew 3:13</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">That he might be baptized by him.</hi> For what purpose did the Son of God wish to be baptized? This may be learned, in some measure, from his answer. We have already assigned a special reason. He received the same baptism with us, in order to assure believers, that they are ingrafted into his body, and that they are “buried with him in baptism,” that they may rise to “newness of life,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4">Romans 6:4</reference>.) But the end, which he here proposes, is more <hi type="italic">extensive: for thus it became him to fulfill all righteousness, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.15">verse 15</reference>.) The word <hi type="italic">righteousness </hi>frequently signifies, in Scripture, the observation of the law: and in that sense we may explain this passage to mean that, since Christ had voluntarily subjected himself to the law, it was necessary that he should keep it in every part. But I prefer a more simple interpretation. “Say nothing for the present,” said our Lord, “about my rank: <note n="292"> <div sID="gen96757" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Je laisse maintenant ma dignite a part</foreign>.” — “I now lay my rank aside.”<div eID="gen96757" type="x-p"/> </note> for the question before us is not, which of us deserves to be placed above the other. <note n="293"> <div sID="gen96758" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Lequel de nous deux est plus grand ou excellent</foreign>;” — “which of usboth is greater or more excellent.”<div eID="gen96758" type="x-p"/> </note> Let us rather consider what our calling demands, and what has been enjoined on us by God the Father.” The general reason why Christ received baptism was, that he might render full obedience to the Father; and the special reason was, that he might consecrate baptism in his own body, that we might have it in common with him.<div eID="gen96756" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96755" osisID="Matt.3.13" type="section"/>
entries.c456f39e352c04c27ba49f014f4ad6202e0d0d4d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.14" sID="gen96759" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14. </hi><hi type="italic">I have need to be baptized by thee.</hi> It is certain, that John acknowledged Christ to be not only a distinguished prophet, as many foolishly dream, but the Son of God, as he really was: for otherwise he would have dishonored God by lowering his holy calling to a mortal man. How he came to know this, the reader will learn by consulting John’s Gospel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.15 Bible:John.1.33">1:15,33.</reference>) There was, no doubt, plausibility in this ground of refusal, that Christ had no need of his baptism: but John was mistaken in not considering, that it was for the sake of others that baptism was asked. <note n="294"> <div sID="gen96761" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que c'est pour le profit des autres, et non pas pour le sien, que Christ demande d'estre baptize</foreign>.” — “That it is for the benefit of others, and not for his own, that Christ asks to be baptized.”<div eID="gen96761" type="x-p"/> </note> And so Christ bids him consider, what was suitable to the character of a <hi type="italic">servant</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.7">Philippians 2:7</reference>,) which he had undertaken; for a voluntary subjection takes nothing from his glory. Though the good man <note n="295"> <div sID="gen96762" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quelque excellent personnage qu'il fust</foreign>.” — “However excellent a person he was.”<div eID="gen96762" type="x-p"/> </note> remained ignorant, for a time, of some part of his public duty, this particular error did not prevent him from discharging, in a proper and lawful manner, his office of Baptist. This example shows, that we do not act rashly, in undertaking the commission which the Lord has given us, according to the light we enjoy, though we do not immediately comprehend all that belongs to our calling, or that depends upon it. We must also observe his modesty, in giving up his opinion, and immediately obeying Christ.<div eID="gen96760" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96759" osisID="Matt.3.14" type="section"/>
entries.d35c336e3a43781d0d2958679a885bf94289ad05: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.3.16" sID="gen96763" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16. </hi><hi type="italic">And, lo, the heavens were opened to him.</hi> <hi type="italic">The opening of the heavens</hi> sometimes means a manifestation of heavenly glory; but here it means also a <hi type="italic">cleft, or opening, </hi>of the visible heaven, so that John could see something beyond the planets and stars. The words of Mark can have no other meaning, <hi type="italic">he saw the heavens cleft asunder</hi> <note n="296"> <div sID="gen96765" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Il vid les cieux mi-partir, </hi>ou se fendre</foreign>.” — “<hi type="italic">He saw the heavens divided in the middle, </hi>or deft.”<div eID="gen96765" type="x-p"/> </note> An exact inquiry into the way in which this opening was made, would be of no importance, nor is it necessary. It is sufficient for us to believe, that it was a symbol of the Divine presence. As the Evangelists say that John saw the Holy Spirit, it is probable that the <hi type="italic">opening of the heavens </hi>was chiefly on his account. Yet I do not hesitate to admit that Christ also, so far as he was man, received from it additional certainty as to his heavenly calling. This appears to be the tendency of the words of Luke: <hi type="italic">while Jesus was praying, the heaven was opened</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.21">Luke 3:21</reference>:) for, though his prayers were always directed towards the benefit of others, yet as man, when he commenced a warfare of so arduous a description, he needed to be armed with a remarkable power of the Spirit.<div eID="gen96764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96766" type="x-p"/>But here two questions arise. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> is, why did the Spirit, who had <hi type="italic">formerly</hi> dwelt in Christ, descend upon <hi type="italic">him at that time? </hi>This question is answered by a passage of the prophet Isaiah, which will be handled in another place.<div eID="gen96766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96767" type="x-p"/>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord God hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the broken-hearted,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.1">Isaiah 61:1</reference>.)<div eID="gen96767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96768" type="x-p"/>Though the grace of the Spirit was bestowed on Christ in a remarkable and extraordinary manner, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.34">John 3:34</reference>,) yet he remained at home as a private person, till he should be called to public life by the Father. Now that the full time is come, for preparing to discharge the office of Redeemer, he is clothed with a new power of the Spirit, and that not so much for his own sake, as for the sake of others. It was done on purpose, that believers might learn to receive, and to contemplate with reverence, his divine power, and that the weakness of the flesh might not make him despised.<div eID="gen96768" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.3.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96763" osisID="Matt.3.16" type="section"/>

17. And, lo, a voice from heaven From that opening of the heavens, which has been already mentioned, a loud voice was heard, that its majesty might be more impressive. The public appearance of Christ, to undertake the office of Mediator, was accompanied by this announcement,
“Avec ce tesmoignage et recommandation;” — “with this testimony and recommendation.”
in which he was offered to us by the Father, that we may rely on this pledge of our adoption, and boldly call God himself our Father. The designation of Son belongs truly and naturally to Christ alone: but yet he was declared to be the Son of God in our flesh, that the favor of Him, whom he alone has a right to call Father, may be also obtained for us. And thus when God presents Christ to us as Mediator, accompanied by the title of Son, he declares that he is the Father of us all, (Ephesians 4:6.)
Such, too, is the import of the epithet beloved: for in ourselves we are hateful to God, and his fatherly love must flow to us by Christ. The best expounder of this passage is the Apostle Paul, when he says
“who hath predestinated us into adoption by Jesus Christ in himself, according to the good pleasure of his will; to the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he hath accepted us in the Beloved,” (Ephesians 1:5,6)
that is, in his beloved Son. It is still more fully expressed by these words, in whom I am well pleased They imply, that the love of God rests on Christ in such a manner, as to diffuse itself from him to us all; and not to us only, but even to the angels themselves. Not that they need reconciliation, for they never were at enmity with God: but even they become perfectly united to God, only by means of their Head, (Ephesians 1:22.) For the same reason, he is also called “the first-born of every creature,” (Colossians 1:5;) and Paul likewise states that Christ came
“to reconcile all things to himself, both those which are on earth, and those which are in heavens,” (Colossians 1:20.)

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:222" />3 For this is he that was spoken of by the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is not much material, whether we understand these words, as the words of the <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi> concerning <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> as it should seem by <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 1.3. and <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 3.4. or the words of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, for he thus spake, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.23. As the words of the <ns0:hi>Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet</ns0:hi> they are found, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 40.3. The words are judged <ns0:hi>Lite<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rally,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Typically</ns0:hi> to concern <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Darius,</ns0:hi> and either these <ns0:hi>Princes,</ns0:hi> who were Instrumental in the restoring of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> to their Liberty from the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> or those <ns0:hi>Prophets</ns0:hi> who incouraged them to their return, or upon their return to build the Temple, and City. But they are con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmed by all the four <ns0:hi>Evangelists, Mar.</ns0:hi> 1.3. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 3.4. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.23. to have a special Relation also to <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> who was to come more immediately before Christ, and with the <ns0:hi>Fervency,</ns0:hi> and in the <ns0:hi>Spirit of Elias, Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.17. cry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, <ns0:hi>Prepare you the way of the Lord, make his Paths strait,</ns0:hi> as the Harbingers of great <ns0:hi>Princes</ns0:hi> are sent before them to call to Persons, to remove things out of the way which may hinder their free Passage, so <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was sent before this great <ns0:hi>King in Zion,</ns0:hi> now coming forth to shew himself, and to set up his Kingdom in the World; to <ns0:hi>Cry fervently</ns0:hi> to all People by a true and timely Repentance, to cast off those sinful Courses, and to reject those false Opinions, of which they were possessed, the holding of and to which, might hinder the Progress of this spiritual Kingdom.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 1.6.</ns0:note> same John had his rayment of Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mels hair, and a leathern girdle about his loyns, and his meat was locusts and wild honey.<ns0:note place="bottom">There are great and insignificant Disputes, about the <ns0:hi>Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bit,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Diet</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptist.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> doubtless designed no more, then to let us know, that <ns0:hi>Iohn Baptist's Habit</ns0:hi> was not of <ns0:hi>soft Rayment,</ns0:hi> like those who are in <ns0:hi>Princes Houses,</ns0:hi> but a plain Country Habit, suited to the <ns0:hi>Place</ns0:hi> in which he lived, and his <ns0:hi>Diet</ns0:hi> plain, such as the Country afforded. In vain therefore do some contend that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> wore <ns0:hi>watered Stuff,</ns0:hi> fine and splendid, as Art in our days hath improved <ns0:hi>Camels Hair</ns0:hi>; and others as vainly contend, that he went in a <ns0:hi>Camels skin</ns0:hi> raw, and undrel<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> But he was habited in a plain Sute of <ns0:hi>Camels Hair,</ns0:hi> such as ordinary Persons of that Country used, or else such a rough Garment as is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Zach.</ns0:hi> 13.4. used by the Prophets. <ns0:hi>Elijah</ns0:hi> had much such an Habit, 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 1.8. There is like wise a Variety of Opinions about these <ns0:hi>Locusts,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> did eat, the most probable is, that they were true <ns0:hi>Locusts,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Locusts</ns0:hi> might be eaten, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 11.22. Nor is it to be thought that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> did eat nothing else, all that is intended is, to let us know that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was a man not at all Curious as to his <ns0:hi>Meat</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Clothes,</ns0:hi> but was Habited plainly, and fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />red ordinarily, as the Men of that Country fared, if there were any Difference in his Habit, it was to Proportion himself to <ns0:hi>Elijah,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Habit of Prophets.</ns0:hi> In this the Evangelist teacheth us what the Ministers of the Gospel should be, and do. They should be Men contemning the Gawdry, and Delicacies of the World, and by their <ns0:hi>Habit</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Diet,</ns0:hi> as well as other things set an Example, of Severity, and Gravity to others.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 1.5.</ns0:note> Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judea, and all the Region round about Jordan.<ns0:note place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Preacher</ns0:hi> being described, the <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi> proceedeth to tell us what Auditors he had. The term <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> here twice re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peated, is enough to let us know, that it is often in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture significative, no further then <ns0:hi>Many,</ns0:hi> for it cannot be ima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gined, that every individual Person in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gion</ns0:hi> about <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> went to hear <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptist,</ns0:hi> but a great many did: It is not to be admired that there went out such a Con-course of People to hear <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptist.</ns0:hi> 1. If it be true, that from <ns0:hi>Ezra's</ns0:hi> time till now, no Prophet had appeared: Our Saviour speaking of <ns0:hi>Iohn, what went you out for to see? A Prophet</ns0:hi>? Seems to hint that a <ns0:hi>Prophet</ns0:hi> was a great Rarity amongst them. 2. If we consider the <ns0:hi>Severity of his Life.</ns0:hi> Our Saviour saith he came neither eating or drinking, that is as other Men. 3. If we consider the new Doctrine he brought, and his Fervency in the pressing it, he came to Preach the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> whom the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had long expected; to tell them his Kingdom was at hand. 4. Especially if we consider the new Rite of <ns0:hi>Baptizing,</ns0:hi> which he brought in. For admit their washing of <ns0:hi>Proselytes</ns0:hi> in use before, yet he <ns0:hi>baptized Iews. He was sent</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Baptize with Water, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.33. So as from his time the <ns0:hi>Institution</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Sacrament</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> must be dated, and he did <ns0:hi>Baptize</ns0:hi> many.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And were Baptized of him in Jordan con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fessing their Sins.<ns0:note place="bottom">A great part of those who went out to hear <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>Baptized,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>Dipped</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> but from hence it will not follow, that <ns0:hi>Dipping</ns0:hi> is Essential to <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi>: The wash<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Soul with the Blood of Christ (the thing signified by Baptism) being expressed by <ns0:hi>sprinkling</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>pouring Water,</ns0:hi> as well as by <ns0:hi>Dipping,</ns0:hi> or being <ns0:hi>buried in Water, Isa.</ns0:hi> 44.3. <ns0:hi>Ezeck.</ns0:hi> 36.25. <ns0:hi>Coloss.</ns0:hi> 2.12. whether they confessed their Sins, Man by Man, by word of Mouth, or by submitting to the Doctrine of the Gospel declared, their Renunciation of the Righteousness of the Law, and their Ingagement to an Holy Life is not expressed. But it is most certain, that a Profe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sion of Faith and Repentance, was ordinarily required before the <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>adult Persons.</ns0:hi> It may be admired that this new Practice of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> (if it were wholly new) made no more stir amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi> Either (as some think) <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> was in use before that time, as an Appendex to <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> (tho Circumcision only be mentioned) or they had some No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion that <ns0:hi>Christ, Elias</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>that Prophet,</ns0:hi> when they came should Baptize: For <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.25. they asked <ns0:hi>Iohn? Why Bap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tizest thou then, if thou be not that Christ, nor Elias, nor that Prophet.</ns0:hi> That which seemeth to me most probable is, That before that time there was a <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> in ordinary use amongst them after <ns0:hi>Circumcising the Child,</ns0:hi> beside the <ns0:hi>Baptizing of Proselytes.</ns0:hi> And as in the other Sacrament, Christ left out the <ns0:hi>Typical part,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Blessed</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Bread,</ns0:hi> used at last in that <ns0:hi>Administration,</ns0:hi> and made use of that for the Institution of the Sacrament of the <ns0:hi>Supper</ns0:hi>: So as to the Ordinance of <ns0:hi>Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumcision,</ns0:hi> he in the Institution of that Gospel-Ordinance, left out <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> (which was <ns0:hi>Typical also,</ns0:hi> and retained only the <ns0:hi>washing of the Person with Water,</ns0:hi> and so instituted the other Sacrament of the <ns0:hi>New Testament.</ns0:hi> But yet there was so much new in the <ns0:hi>Baptists Practice</ns0:hi> (for he did not bap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tize <ns0:hi>Proselytes</ns0:hi> only, but <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> nor did he use it as an Ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pendix to Circumcision preceeding, but baptized adult <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>) that if the State of the <ns0:hi>Iewish Church</ns0:hi> had not been declining, and their Power of Discipline very little (if any) they would more then have sent to <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> to know by whose Authority he <ns0:hi>Baptized</ns0:hi>: But they were under the <ns0:hi>Roman Power,</ns0:hi> and their <ns0:hi>Ecclesiastical Officers,</ns0:hi> were more Pragmatical, then mischievous God in the Wisdom of his Providence, having so ordered it that the <ns0:hi>Change of Worship</ns0:hi> should be at such a time brought in, when it should be least potently opposed.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 But when he saw many of the Pharisees, and Sadduces come to his Baptism, he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 3.7.</ns0:note> O Generation of Vipers, who hath warned you to flee from <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 5.5<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 1 Thes. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> the wrath to come.<ns0:note place="bottom">We shall often meet with the mention of these <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sad<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ces</ns0:hi>: We will therefore inquire here a little more largely concerning them. There were three more eminent Religious Sects amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Essenes</ns0:hi> of whom we read nothing in Holy-writ, their main Doctrine was <ns0:hi>Fate,</ns0:hi> they ascribed all things to it. The two others are here mentioned, and often, in other parts of the New Testament, we read of the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sadduces</ns0:hi>: The latter were most acceptable to the great Men amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> the former were more Popular, and acceptable to the People. The <ns0:hi>Sadduces,</ns0:hi> were directly opposite to the <ns0:hi>Essenes,</ns0:hi> they ascribed nothing to Fate, but maintained the Liberty and Power of mans Will in the most Extravagant height, they denyed the <ns0:hi>Immortality of the Soul,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Resurrection, Angels,</ns0:hi> &c. all which the <ns0:hi>Pharises</ns0:hi> owned, this we may learn from <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 23.8. where <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> wrought his own Escape by setting these two Factions on quarrelling about these Points. In short these were no better then <ns0:hi>Athiests</ns0:hi> (for what must they be less that deny <ns0:hi>Spirits,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Resurrection</ns0:hi>?) The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> as to their Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine, were much more sober, they owned <ns0:hi>Spirits,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Resurrection,</ns0:hi> and tho they held much of the Freedom of, and a Power in mans Will; yet they also ascribed much to the <ns0:hi>Providence</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> of God: They were the <ns0:hi>Interpreters</ns0:hi> of the Law, and as Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin</ns0:hi> thinks, had their Name from thence, not from their dividing and separating themselves from others (as some think) they spent much of their time in Fasting and Prayer, but, 1. <ns0:hi>They held a Righteousness by the Works of the Law, to be our Righteousness, for which we are accepted of God.</ns0:hi> 2. They made a very <ns0:hi>jejune Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation</ns0:hi> of the Law, as may appear from our Saviours Cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />recting it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 5. 3. <ns0:hi>They held many unwritten Traditi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of equal Force with the Law of God.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>Fourthly,</ns0:hi> they <ns0:hi>were very Hypocrites in their Practice,</ns0:hi> neglecting the weigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty things of the Law, making long Prayers for a Pretence for their wickedness, and doing all they did, but to be seen of men. Some of these <ns0:hi>Sadduces</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> came to <ns0:hi>Iohn's Baptism,</ns0:hi> and no wonder, for <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 6.20. <ns0:hi>Herod observed him, heard him, did many things, and heard him gladly,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 7.30. it is said the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were not <ns0:hi>Baptized of him.</ns0:hi> It is like they came out of Curiosity [He <ns0:hi>said unto them, O Generation of Vipers</ns0:hi>] the very Language which Christ used to them, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.34. and 23.33. The <ns0:hi>Viper</ns0:hi> to which he compareth them, is the worst and most dangerous of Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pents: We need give no Account of the <ns0:hi>Baptists</ns0:hi> treating them so roughly, because our Saviour justifieth the term by applying it to them. <ns0:hi>Corrupt Teachers</ns0:hi> are the worst of Men, and of all orders of Sinners, fewest of them <ns0:hi>Repent</ns0:hi> and have their Hearts changed [<ns0:hi>who hath warned you to flee from the Wrath to come</ns0:hi>] what comes in your mind, who think there is <ns0:hi>no Resurrection, no Hell,</ns0:hi> or who think you are so righteous that you need fear none, to do any thing that might testifie you are afraid of Wrath to come.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:222" />8 Bring forth therefore fruits meet <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>answera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to amend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> for re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pentance.<ns0:note place="bottom">You come here and thrust your selves into a Crowd of Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nitents, but this is not enough, true Repentance is not a barren thing, neither are your leaves of external Profe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sion a sufficient Indication of it, you must bring forth the Fruits of Holiness, Fruits that may answer the Nature of true Repentance. The proper Products of Habits, are called their Fruits, thus we read of the <ns0:hi>Fruit of Sin,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Fruit of Righteousness, Fruits meet for Repentance</ns0:hi>; are Works that are the proper Product of Repentance, or justly answering an external Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of Repentance. As <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>Repentance without Works</ns0:hi> is dead.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And think not to say within your selves, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 8.33. Act. 13.26.</ns0:note> we have Abraham to <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> Father: For I say unto you that God is able of these stones to raise up chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren unto Abraham.<ns0:note place="bottom">All Hypocrites bear up themselves upon something, upon which they Promise good to themselves, and a Freedom from the Judgments of God. The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> rested much upon their Descent from <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> as appeareth also from <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.39. by which means they intituled themselves to the Covenant, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17. extended <ns0:hi>to his Seed,</ns0:hi> as well as to himself, as also to the Name of the <ns0:hi>Church, Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Posterity by <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> being all the visible Church, which God had upon the Earth at that time: It is the great work of Ministers to drive Hypocrites from their vain Confidences. This <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> doth here, as if he should say, I know what you trust too, you think with your selves; that, because you are the only Church of God upon the Earth, Judgment shall not come upon you, God would then have no Seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> to shew Mercy to, and to keep his Covenant with, but mistake not, God of stones if he please can raise up <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> to keep Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant with <ns0:hi>Papists,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Formalists</ns0:hi> have much the same Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumption, tho with this difference, The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were the true, the only Church of God, these do but arrogate the Name to themselves.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And now also the Ax is laid to the root of the trees, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 15.6, 7.</ns0:note> therefore, every tree which, bring<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth not forth good <ns0:hi>fruit,</ns0:hi> is hewn down, and cast into the fire.<ns0:note place="bottom">A Prediction as some think, of that dreadful <ns0:hi>Destruction,</ns0:hi> which within a few years came by the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> upon the whole <ns0:hi>Iewish Nation.</ns0:hi> The Sense is: The Vengeance of God is very near to be revealed, Men must <ns0:hi>Repent Now</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Never,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>every Tree which bringeth not forth good Fruit shall be hewn down, and cast into the Fire,</ns0:hi> Judgment now is as nigh unto Men, as the Tree is to falling, to the Root of which the Ax is already applyed, whether it be to be understood of the Judgment common to all unbelievers, all that <ns0:hi>know not God, and obey not the Gospel of Christ,</ns0:hi> as 2 <ns0:hi>Thessal.</ns0:hi> 1.8, 9. or the particular Destruction of this Nation of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> I shall not determine, tho I rather judge the latter probable. The latter part of the Text is made use of by our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.19. in the latter part of his Sermon upon the Mountain. It letteth us know, that it is not Improper, nor Dissonant to the Stile of <ns0:hi>Iohn Baptist,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> and others the most eminent first Gospel-Preachers, to press <ns0:hi>Repentance, Faith,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Holiness of Life, from Arguments of Terror.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 I indeed Baptize you with water <ns0:note place="margin">Act 1.5. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 1.16. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note> unto Repentance, but he that cometh after me, is mightier then I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear, he shall baptize you with the holy ghost, and <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> fire.<ns0:note place="bottom">I am not the Christ, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 1.8. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 3.15.16. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.15.26. I am but the Messenger, and forerunner of Christ sent be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore him, to Baptize men with the <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> of Water, in Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stimony of their <ns0:hi>Repentance,</ns0:hi> but there is one immediately coming after me, who is infinitely to be preferred before me, so much, that I am not worthy to carry his Shoes, or un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loose his Shoe-latchet: He shall <ns0:hi>Baptize</ns0:hi> men with another kind of <ns0:hi>Baptism,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptisme</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Holy Ghost</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Fire. With the Holy Ghost</ns0:hi> inwardly washing away their Sins with his Blood, and sanctifying their Hearts, the Holy Ghost work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing in their Hearts like Fire, purging out their Lusts and Cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruptions, <ns0:hi>warming</ns0:hi> and inflaming their Hearts with the Sense of his Love, and kindling in them all spiritual Habits, or <ns0:hi>with the Holy Ghost,</ns0:hi> as in the days of <ns0:hi>Pentecost, there appearing to them cloven Tongues like as of Fire,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 2.3. thus the term <ns0:hi>Fire</ns0:hi> is made Exegetical of the term [the <ns0:hi>Holy Ghost</ns0:hi>] Or <ns0:hi>with the Holy Ghost, and with Fire,</ns0:hi> changing and renew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Hearts of those that believe in him, by the Operation of the Holy Ghost, and consuming and destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing others, that will not believe, as with <ns0:hi>Fire.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Whose fan <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to his garner: but will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> is at present Gods floor, the only Church he hath upon the Earth, but there is Chaff upon this floor, as well as Wheat. Now he is <ns0:hi>come,</ns0:hi> who will make a <ns0:hi>Separation,</ns0:hi> betwixt the <ns0:hi>Chaff</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Wheat</ns0:hi>: Who by his <ns0:hi>Preaching the Gospel</ns0:hi> will distinguish betwixt <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and those that are of <ns0:hi>Israel, Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.6. betwixt those who living in the true Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pectation of the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> shall receive him now he is come, and those that by their not owning and receiving him, shall declare that they never had any true Expectation of him, shall separate them into distinct <ns0:hi>Heaps,</ns0:hi> raising up a Go<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>pel Church, and shall at the last day make yet a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rict Discrimi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation, and througly Purge his floor, taking true Believers in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to Heaven, and burning Unbelievers with <ns0:hi>unquenchable Fire,</ns0:hi> casting them into Torments like unquenchable F<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>re.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 1.9. Luk. 3.21.</ns0:note> Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dan unto John to be baptized of him.<ns0:note place="bottom">Christ who now was about thirty years of Age, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 3.23. cometh from <ns0:hi>Nazareth</ns0:hi> a City in <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi> where <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> lived, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.4. and whither he went with <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary, Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.39. and again after he had Disputed with the <ns0:hi>Doctors</ns0:hi> at twelve years of Age, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.46. cometh from thence to <ns0:hi>Ior<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dan</ns0:hi> the great River, where <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ptizing Disciples, offering himself to be Baptized of him. He shewed his Hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mility by going to him, and also made the Action publick. If any ask to what end Christ, who had no sin was Baptized, himself gives us an Account, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.5. <ns0:hi>To fulfil all Righteousness</ns0:hi> (of which more in its place) He thus owned <ns0:hi>Iohns</ns0:hi> Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stry and Mission to <ns0:hi>Baptize,</ns0:hi> and confirmed the <ns0:hi>Institution of Baptism</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Water,</ns0:hi> and offered himself to that Testimony, which he knew his Father would give of him. He thus ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiated himself in the Christian Church, as by <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> he had made himself of the <ns0:hi>Iewish Church,</ns0:hi> and so was both the Head of the believing <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles.</ns0:hi> He was not (as others) Baptized in Testimony of his <ns0:hi>Repentance,</ns0:hi> or for the <ns0:hi>Remission of sins,</ns0:hi> for he was <ns0:hi>without sin.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 But John forbad him saying, I have need to be baptized of thee and comest thou to me?<ns0:note place="bottom">He did not absolutely repel him, but modestly excused him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self for a time, knowing that Christ was already baptized with a more excellent <ns0:hi>Baptism,</ns0:hi> then he could Administer to him, <ns0:hi>for God gave him the Spirit not by Measure, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.34.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15. And Jesus answering said unto him, suffer <ns0:hi>it to be so</ns0:hi> now; for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iesus</ns0:hi> saith unto him. <ns0:hi>Suffer it now to be so.</ns0:hi> The Question is not whether thou or I be more <ns0:hi>Excellent</ns0:hi>: It is thy Duty to <ns0:hi>Baptize</ns0:hi> for my Father hath sent thee to <ns0:hi>Baptize.</ns0:hi> It is my Pleasure and Duty to be Obedient to my Father, whose Will I know tho it be hidden from thee. <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> is a new Law of the Gospel-Church, of which tho I be the Head, yet I must be conformed to the Members of it, concerning which my Fathers Will is, that they should be <ns0:hi>Baptized with Water,</ns0:hi> as well as with the <ns0:hi>Holy Ghost,</ns0:hi> besides that, I am to put an end to the Jewish Typical <ns0:hi>Circumcision,</ns0:hi> and to put a new Face upon the Church, by Instituting ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Sacrament of Initiation. It is therefore both <ns0:hi>Iust</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Equal</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>I should be Baptized,</ns0:hi> (tho not for those ends for which others, that are my Members, are Baptized, not for Remission of sins, but) for the fulfilling of all Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness, in obeying my Fathers Will [<ns0:hi>So he suffered him</ns0:hi>] he that erreth through ignorance will correct his Error upon better Information. We may learn from this Example of Christ. That being <ns0:hi>Baptized with the Holy Ghost,</ns0:hi> will excuse none for <ns0:hi>Contempt,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Neglect</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Water,</ns0:hi> because it is the revealed Will of God, that all the Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers of his Church should come under that Ordinance, so as there is a <ns0:hi>fulfilling of Righteousness</ns0:hi> in our Case, as well as in Christ's, tho in a different measure.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And Jesus, when he was Baptized, went up straight way out of the water, and lo the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 11.2. Joh. 1.32.33.</ns0:note> the Spirit of God descending like a Dove, and lighting up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And lo a voice from heaven saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 2.7. Isa. 42.1. <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 12.18. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 17.5. Luk. 9.35. Col. 1.13.</ns0:note> This is my Beloved Son in whom I am well pleased.<ns0:note place="bottom">This story is also related by <ns0:hi>Mar</ns0:hi> 1.10, 11. and by <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 3.21. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith that <ns0:hi>Iesus praying the Heavens were opened. Mark</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>cloven asunder.</ns0:hi> It is most probable, that the opening of the Heavens mentioned, (tho possibly far more Glorious) bare a Proportion to that <ns0:hi>opening of the Heavens,</ns0:hi> which we often see in a time of great Light<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning, when the Air seemeth to divide to make the fuller, and clearer way for the Light [<ns0:hi>unto him</ns0:hi>] that is unto <ns0:hi>Iohn [and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a Dove, and lighting upon him]</ns0:hi> The Spirit of God is an invisible Substance, and cannot be seen by <ns0:hi>Humane Eyes,</ns0:hi> but the shape assumed by any Person of the <ns0:hi>Trinity</ns0:hi> may be seen, whether it was a <ns0:hi>real Dove,</ns0:hi> or only the appearance of a <ns0:hi>Dove,</ns0:hi> is little material for us to know. It was certainly one or the other, nor could any Representation at this time be more fit; either, to let the World know the <ns0:hi>Dove like Nature</ns0:hi> of Christ, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 42.2. or what should be the Temper of all those who receive the same Sp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rit, tho by measure, and are by it taught to be <ns0:hi>innocent as Doves,</ns0:hi> not that Christ had not received the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit before<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but that his receiving of it might be notified to others. This <ns0:hi>Dove</ns0:hi> or appearance of a <ns0:hi>Dove</ns0:hi> lighted upon Christ, thereby shewing for whose sake this <ns0:hi>Apparition</ns0:hi> was<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Christ was not confirmed only to be the Son of God by this appearance of the <ns0:hi>Holy Spirit,</ns0:hi> in the form of a <ns0:hi>Dove,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>lighting</ns0:hi> upon him, but also by a <ns0:hi>Voice</ns0:hi> from the <ns0:hi>Excellent Glory</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.17. God forming a Voice in the Air which spake saying: <ns0:hi>This is</ns0:hi> my <ns0:hi>beloved Son in whom I am well pleased.</ns0:hi> The word signifieth, a <ns0:hi>dearly beloved Son.</ns0:hi> The same Voice was repeated at Christ's <ns0:hi>Transfiguration, Mat.</ns0:hi> 17.5. <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> from it concludes the certainty of the Faith of the Gospel, in the aforementioned Text [<ns0:hi>In whom I am well pleased</ns0:hi>] The word signifieth a special and singular Complacency, and Satisfaction, I am pleased in his Person, ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to that, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 8.30. I am well pleased in his <ns0:hi>undertaking</ns0:hi> in all that he shall do and suffer in the Accomplishment of the Redemption of Man: <ns0:hi>We are made accepted in the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loved. Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.6. This Text (as is generally observed) is a clear Proof of the <ns0:hi>Trinity</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Persons,</ns0:hi> or Subsistences in the one Divine being: Here was the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> speaking from Heaven, The <ns0:hi>Son baptized</ns0:hi> and come out of the Water. The <ns0:hi>Holy Ghost</ns0:hi> descending in the form or shape of a <ns0:hi>Dove.</ns0:hi>
